<page-num>79</page-num>
<header>PART ONE, TRACTATE IV.</header>

---

# FOLLOWS THE
# PROCESS FOR THE STONE
## of the Philosophers, by a Certain Anonymous Monk.

### First, one makes the PHILOSOPHERS’ VINEGAR.

Take three measures of good wine vinegar and distill it seven times, so it becomes a clear water of Vinegar. Take one measure of this and add a handful <note>original Latin: "manip." (manipulus).</note> of prepared salt. Distill them together, and it will become a beautiful, clear water. This belongs to the Art and dissolves the <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "Leichnam." In alchemy, "corpses" or "bodies" refers to the solid metals before they are dissolved into a liquid state.</note> and turns them into water. Keep this, and place a leaf of silver or gold within it. Add the <term>Quintessence of Wine</term> <note>original Latin: "Q. Essentiam Vini." This usually refers to highly concentrated alcohol or brandy distilled multiple times.</note> to it, and it will become all the more noble and better. The Salt of the Philosophers is drawn out of <term>Luna</term> <note>Latin for the Moon, the alchemical name for Silver.</note> with distilled Vinegar.

## WATER OF MERCURY.

Take twelve <term>loth</term> <note>A traditional German unit of weight, roughly 15-16 grams or half an ounce.</note> of Mercury of Silver <note>Mercury that has been "animated" or refined using silver.</note>, put it in a glass, and pour this Vinegar over it so that it is covered. Place it in a <term>MB</term> <note>Abbreviation for "Balneum Mariae" or Mary's Bath; a double boiler used for gentle, consistent heating.</note> for three days, and it will dissolve the Mercury into a beautiful, pure water. This is the Water of Mercury, the true living silver, and it is the <term>First Matter</term> <note>original Latin: "Prima Materia." The primitive, formless base of all matter that alchemists sought to isolate.</note>, the <term>Virgin’s Milk</term> <note>original Latin: "Lac Virginis." A name for a milky-white alchemical solvent.</note>, the Fountain of the Philosophers; and it has many other names: Water of Life <note>original Latin: "Aqua Vitae."</note>, Salt of Metals, White Eagle, Basilisk, Serpent-bearer, or Serpent-born.

## SOLUTION OF THE SUN.

Take four loth of pure <term>Sol</term> <note>Latin for the Sun, the alchemical name for Gold.</note> beaten thin; put this into a small flask and pour a finger’s breadth of the preceding water over it. Seal the glass at the top and place it in the MB for three days and nights. Two ducats' weight of the gold will dissolve into the water and become a beautiful, true Gold-water. Then pour off this Gold-water from the undissolved gold and pour more of the Mercurial water a finger’s breadth over it again. Place it back in the MB for three days and nights to dissolve. Pour off the dissolved Gold-water and do this a third time until all the gold is dissolved. Put all the Gold-water together in a well-sealed glass; thus you have prepared the two waters of Mercury and the Sun to generate the Stone of Mastery. Here is the King in his bath in the pure, clear fountain, of which <term>Count Bernard of Trevisan</term> <note>A famous 15th-century Italian alchemist known for his allegorical stories about the "King" (Gold) dissolving in a "fountain" (solvent).</note> writes and calls his Little Fountain <note>original Latin: "Fontinam."</note>.

# THE CONJUNCTION OF BOTH WATERS,
# and it is called THE PEARL.

So take four parts of the <term>Mercurial</term> <note>original Latin: "Mercurialis." Referring to the refined mercury water described on the previous page.</note> water of the living <term>Moon</term> <note>original Latin: "Lunae." The alchemical name for Silver.</note> and one part of the dissolved <term>Gold-water</term>; put them together in a <term>separating flask</term> <note>original German: "scheydkolben." A glass vessel used for distillation or separation.</note> and place it in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original abbreviation: "MB." for Balneum Mariae (Mary’s Bath). A gentle double-boiler system.</note> for four days and nights in a constant warmth. Take care that it does not grow cold; thus the components will <term>digest</term> <note>The process of slow heating to encourage chemical reaction.</note> together and become of one nature and property. This is the <term>Fountain of the Philosophers</term> <note>original Latin: "Fons Philosophorum." A common metaphor for the liquid state from which the Philosopher's Stone emerges.</note>, within which the Stone is hidden.

## Now follows: How one shall separate the four
## elements from the water.

Take the glass with the water, place a <term>still-head</term> <note>original German: "Helm," literally "helmet." The cap of a distillation apparatus that collects vapor.</note> upon it, and distill it <term>by the water bath</term> <note>original Latin: "per Baln."</note> for three days and nights. When the <term>Matter</term> <note>original Latin: "Materia."</note> rises, it is the element of Water, and it is a beautiful, clear water. This is the first element, the <term>Spirit of the Body</term> <note>original German: "Geist deß Leichnams." Alchemists viewed the volatile parts of a substance as its spirit, leaving the "corpse" or solid matter behind.</note>. A dark <term>matter</term> remains at the bottom. Guard the water well, for with this water all things are prepared and completed; it is the <term>First Matter</term> <note>original Latin: "prima Materia." The formless, primordial substance required to create the Stone.</note> of the Stone.

## The second element: AIR.

Take the glass with the dark substance at the bottom; place it in a <term>sand bath</term> <note>original German: "Capell." Literally a cupel, but here used as a vessel for heating in ashes.</note> with ashes, and <term>seal it tightly</term> <note>original German: "verlutiers." To seal with "lute," a paste or clay used to make joints airtight.</note>. Distill it with a gentle fire, and an oil will distill out. This is the element of Air. What remains at the bottom is a dry substance; this is the <term>Body</term> <note>original Latin: "Corpus."</note> called Earth, the <term>Earth of the Philosophers</term> <note>original Latin: "Terra Philosophorum."</note>. Grind it small and keep it.

## How one shall purge and purify the two
## elements, Water and Air.

Take the element of Water, put it into a flask, and place it for eighteen days in the <term>water bath</term>. Do the same with the other element, the Air; also place it for eighteen days in the <term>bath</term>. Seal the glasses tightly. Afterward, take them and distill each one separately <term>by the water bath</term>. Then, place the two elements on the warm ashes for ten days so that the two elements are distilled and well-purified for the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The final concentrated substance capable of transmuting metals.</note>.

## How one shall now purge the third
## element, the Earth.

Take the third element, the <term>black earth</term> <note>original Latin: "Terram nigram." This represents the stage of "nigredo" or blackness in the alchemical work.</note>; grind it small, and

## How one shall raise the stone into the high
## red color.

## How one shall ferment.

Now take the stone, grind it small, and take the **Element of Air** (three parts of the <term>Oil</term>). Place it in a <term>sand cupel</term> <note>original German: "Sand Capellen." Then take it out and grind it small; then give it the Oil again as before, and set it back upon the ashes and sand. Thus it will rise again with many different colors in the circulatory vessel and will be turned into a beautiful red. And the **Saying of the Philosophers** is fulfilled:
> Our stone rises into heaven, and descends again to the earth,

# AUGMENTATION or MULTIPLI-
## cation and Fixation of the Stone.

So take four <term>loth</term> <note>A German unit of weight, roughly equivalent to half an ounce or 15-16 grams.</note> of <term>Mercury of the Moon</term> <note>original Latin: "Mercurij Lunæ." In the alchemical tradition, this usually refers to silver that has been purified or reduced to a mercurial state.</note> and two loth of <term>leaf gold</term> <note>original Latin: "Solis foliatum." Sol (the Sun) is the alchemical name for gold.</note>, and take one loth of the **blessed Stone**. Grind them together upon a stone; put it into a <term>flask</term> <note>original German: "Kolben." A glass vessel used for distillation.</note> and pour four loth of the first **Element of Water** upon it. Set it upon the sand or ashes and distill from the matter. Then take the flask out, and if it has dissolved, return it again to the bottom of the matter. Take it out and grind it small; put it back into the flask and give it another four loth of the water. Do this seven times, and the matter will become <term>fixed</term> <note>original German: "fir." Meaning the substance is now stable and will no longer evaporate or escape when subjected to heat.</note> and constant. After that, give it the **Element of Air** as often as needed until it becomes fluid like wax, as was mentioned before, until it is again <term>coagulated</term> <note>Solidified from a liquid state.</note> red into a Stone.

# How the Tincture should be multiplied.

So take one hundred loth of crude Mercury, or <term>Antimony</term> <note>Represented by the symbol ♁. Antimony was frequently used in the "cleansing" of metals.</note>, well-purified with salt and <term>vinegar</term> <note>original Latin: "Aceto."</note> three times. Set these in a crucible upon the fire until they begin to crackle (and henceforth to smoke). Then take one loth of the **Tincture**; throw it upon it and blow with the bellows for one hour. Thus the Mercury transforms into a red powder and the medicine is augmented, and you have one hundred loth of medicine from one loth.

From this Tincture, take one loth and throw it upon one hundred parts of crude Mercury or Antimony; thus it will become good Gold, constant in all tests from that moment on. For this, praise and thank God, who reveals this secret to mankind; it is a gift of God.

and bring forth this noble Fifth Essence <note>original: "Q. ESSE." or "Quinta Essentia," the pure, celestial essence hidden within all things.</note>; otherwise, we will be able to accomplish little of value, whether in medicine or in the transmutation of metals <note>original: "Transmutatione metallorum"</note>.

Now, man himself is the fifth essence and is a microcosm <term>Microcosm: From the Greek meaning "little world," the belief that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</term>, taken from the great world, and is the son of the entire universe. We humans eat and drink our flesh and blood from our father—the elements and the firmament—which sounds strange to the ears of the blind, mad world and seems unbelievable to them. But among true philosophers, it requires little wonder or confirmation. Naturalists and practitioners of magic <note>original: "Magi"</note> thank God that this is one of the great wonders of God <note>original: "Magnalibus DEI"</note>, which the godless, blind world does not respect. Instead, like swine, they wallow with their snouts in the filth of temporal, earthly Mammon <term>Mammon: A term used in the New Testament to personify wealth and greed as a false idol.</term>, and they care little to ask about the wonders of God, of nature, and the mysteries hidden within themselves.

Now, it is no different: man is a microcosm and the smaller world, created by God out of the great world. For the clod of earth from which Adam was made consisted of eight parts or substances; this clod of earth was an extract and refinement of the four elements. This refinement was composed of seven substances: Firstly, from the *hyle* <note>original: "Hyle," a Greek term for the primordial, unformed "stuff" of the first matter.</note> or the dust of the first matter. 2. From the water of the sea. 3. From the stones of the earth. 4. From the clouds of the heaven. 5. From the wind. 6. From the sun. 7. From the moon. And the eighth was the living breath, the breath of life <note>original: "Spiraculum vitæ"</note>, breathed by God into the face of the first man; that was the true image of God. And this is the true man; the other seven pieces went into the structure of the human mortal body, in which this divine man and divine spiritual soul was to have its dwelling and residence, like a guest in an inn. Only through Divine will—to those whom dear God wishes to grant it—does He give great understanding in these matters. Once the first [physical body] is broken, we become heirs of a future and present state, where Soul and Spirit are separated from the bodily essence, have been highly purified, and have ascended through **Sublimation** <note>A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, used here as a metaphor for spiritual purification.</note>. Essentiam*; the pure, fifth element or spiritual core of matter.</note> before our eyes, revealed from the two highest **Stars** <note>original: *Astris*; referring to the planets/metals.</note> of the **Sun or Moon** <note>original: *Solis vel Lunæ*; gold or silver.</note>, and their **Sulfur** and **Mercury**, then we would have found the fire of the Sages and the pure, clear Spirit, and overcome the **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note>. And this same thing is now called the Heavenly, Astral, and penetrating fire, and the **Spirit of Life** <note>original: *Spiritus Vitæ*</note>, which is capable of all things and contains everything within itself, to which everything must yield so that everything becomes healthy and pure.

Therefore, the Ancients strove after this heavenly jewel; in this, revelation and great mysteries are hidden. For without this Soul and Spirit—the aforementioned keys—nothing can be accomplished. We need, in life, for the maintenance of health and a long life, the juice of this Soul and this Spirit. It gives our life fiery power; it unlocks all things inwardly, penetrates the inhabitant <note>The "inhabitant" refers to the soul or life-force dwelling within the human body.</note>, refreshes it, and travels through all internal cities <note>A metaphor for the various organs and systems of the body.</note>. It destroys what is evil and preserves what is good. This is the highest intermediary between God and man, the greatest created help in Nature. In it, there is no death, no destructibility, and no combustibility—only fire and a living spirit. This is what the Ancients sought and found, and called the **Fifth Essence**. Through **Viscous** water <note>original: *Viscosam*; likely referring to a thick, oily solvent used in the dissolution process.</note>, it is dissolved and "killed"; through **Sublimation**, it is purified, awakened, made immortal, and born as a **Star** <note>original: *ASTRO*; representing the final, perfected, and "celestial" state of the alchemical matter.</note>.

And this great secret is revealed only to the true **sons of learning** <note>original: *Filiis doctrinæ*; those dedicated to the study of sacred and natural knowledge.</note>, and dear friends of God, who are born by the stars into this art, who love Him, and who seek the Kingdom of God first before all things. Just as each species is assigned its own body, which Nature takes from the **Sulfur**; so too from the **Mercury** she takes each one's **virtues**, as they belong to it.

Therefore, he who wishes to know the **bodies of all things** <note>original: *Corpora rerum omnium*</note> should first know the **Sulfur**. After that, he who wishes to know the **colors** should take the basis for knowing them from the **Salt**. And he who wishes to know the virtues should fathom the secret of **Mercury**; then he will have the foundation to find the **mysteries** <note>original: *Mysteria*</note> in every growing thing.

Now see, dear friends and brothers, thus must one [understand] Nature...

# Preface.

# THE ONE BOOK OF LORENZO VENTURA OF VENICE, DOCTOR OF MEDICINE,
## ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE.

### ->That the art of Alchemy is true.<-

## CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut drop-cap letter 'V' decorated with scrolling foliage and a belt-and-buckle motif.</image-desc>

Many believe that the art of Alchemy is not true, moved to this conclusion by two reasons. First, because Aristotle says in Book 4 of the *Meteorology* <note>original: "lib. 4. meteororum"</note> that the practitioners of Alchemy should know that the forms of metals cannot be changed. Second, because they see that all laborers in this art make nothing but purely deceptive <term>transmutations</term> <note>The supposed transformation of one substance into another, such as lead into gold</note>, and none make a true one. Therefore they think that since they see no one succeeding at it, it cannot be done rightly or truly. 

But neither of these two arguments proves necessarily that this noble and excellent art is untrue. For the first argument of the adversaries has no standing, although it is true as <term>Alphidius</term> and the <term>Greater Rosary</term> <note>original: "Rosarius Major," a highly influential medieval alchemical text</note> say: that the "forms" or essential natures of things cannot be changed. Yet, the individual instances of certain forms can be changed into one another. This is proven by the evidence of our eyes, especially in those things that share a commonality in one or two qualities with each other, as can be seen in the Elements. Thus, from earth comes a stone, and from wood comes ash, and from ash and stones comes glass, etc. 

The same process occurs within metals, since all metals share a single common matter, which is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> with its <term>sulfur</term>. Metals are distinguished from one another only by more or less "cooking," which occurs through the ripeness of their sulfur by means of this cooking. For the sulfur is the form

# LAURENTIUS VENTURA OF VENICE, DOCTOR OF MEDICINE

## *ONE BOOK,*

### ON THE PHILOSOPHER’S STONE.

->That the art of Alchemy is true.<-

->CHAPTER I.<-

<image-desc>Large ornate decorative initial 'V' interlaced with intricate foliage and knotted vine patterns.</image-desc>

Many believe the art of Alchemy is not true, a view they are moved toward by two reasons. First, because Aristotle says in the fourth book of *Meteorology*: the practitioners of Alchemy should know that the forms <note>original: *gestalten*; refers to the Aristotelian 'substantial form' or essential nature of a substance</note> of metals cannot be changed. Secondly, because they see that all workers in this art perform nothing but purely deceptive <note>original: *Sophistische*; referring to fraudulent or superficial chemical imitations</note> transmutations, and no one achieves a true one. Therefore they believe that, since they see it done by no one, it cannot be done rightly and truly.

But it does not necessarily follow from either of these two points that this noble and excellent art is not true. For the first argument of the adversaries has no standing, although it is true as Alphidius <note>An early Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in Western texts</note> and the *Rosarius Major* <note>The "Greater Rosary," a highly influential medieval alchemical compendium</note> say: that the forms of things cannot be changed. However, the individual instances of certain forms can nonetheless be changed into one another. This is proven by outward appearance, especially in those things that share a commonality in one or two qualities with each other, as can be seen in the Elements. Thus, from earth comes a stone, and from wood an ash, and from ashes and stones a glass, etc. 

This is also how it happens with metals, since all metals share a single common matter, which is quicksilver <note>Latin: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note> with its sulfur. And the metals are distinguished only by more or less "cooking" <note>original: *kochung*; the alchemical process of maturation or digestion through heat</note>, which occurs through the ripeness of their sulfur by means of this cooking. For sulfur is the form...

<summary>This page introduces Laurentius Ventura's defense of alchemy, refuting Aristotle's skepticism by arguing that while essential "forms" are fixed, individual substances can be transformed if they share common elements or qualities.</summary>

# THE NEW ROSARY

...of metals, and especially of gold; not indeed the common sulfur, but the altered one, as Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemist from Ferrara, author of the *Precious New Pearl*</note> says. From this it is understood that if a medicine can be made through the Art which possesses within itself the power and property of the aforementioned altered mineral sulfur, then such a medicine is indeed made through Art which can transform imperfect metals and quicksilver into the perfect nature. Therefore, Johannes Scotus <note>Likely referring to a pseudo-epigraphical alchemical work attributed to the philosopher Duns Scotus</note> and other philosophers say and admit that it is quite true that metals cannot be changed by any skill or method unless they are first brought back into their first matter.

The first matter of all metals is <term>Argentum vivum</term> <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; Latin for "living silver," the technical term for mercury or quicksilver</note> and <term>Sulphur</term> <note>Sulfur here refers not to the yellow mineral, but to the "active" or "combustible" principle in the mercury-sulfur theory of metals</note>, though not in their natural state, but altered—that is, turned into a vapor. And thus the first matter of metals is a moist, oily vapor or <term>Vapor</term>, which encompasses the nature of both the Quicksilver and the Sulfur within itself.

From this it necessarily follows that if such an <term>unctuous vapor</term> <note>original: "Vapor unctuosus"; an oily or greasy steam believed to be the substance from which metals grow in the earth</note> or greasy steam can be drawn from those things in which it resides through the Art, and is found to be identical to that which generates metals in the mines of the earth: then a medicine can also be made which can transform simple, imperfect bodies—when cast upon <term>Argentum vivum</term>—into a true and perfect metallic <term>Corpus</term> <note>original: "Corpus"; Latin for body, referring to the solid state of the metal</note>, which will be much more perfect than all natural metals.

It should also be known that this medicine is drawn more easily and abundantly from some things, but with more difficulty and imperfection from others, whether they be the metals themselves or whatever other things they may be. But this cannot happen unless such things are first destroyed through <term>Putrefaction</term> <note>A stage of "rotting" or breakdown intended to strip a substance of its previous form</note> and decay, until through proper cooking and long <term>Digestion</term> <note>A slow, steady heating process meant to mature the substance</note> they receive another, more noble form.

The second reason and argument they cast against us is also not necessary: and this is our response, as Geber <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, traditionally considered the father of alchemy</note> says in his *Summa* <note>Referring to the *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, a foundational alchemical textbook</note> in the second chapter: that just because one looks at a few [failures], it does not follow that our Art is not true. Furthermore, it is certain that in our time very few philosophers are found who recognize the secrets of nature; indeed, they even despise searching for and recognizing them. And therefore they do not know how to improve imperfect things or make them perfect: and generally, they do not know how to separate the useful from the useless, the nearest from the farthest, or the innermost from the outermost. Therefore, many of them err and act unwisely. The ancient Philo- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "sophi" indicates the next page begins with "Philosophers"</note>

It also defends alchemy against skeptics by blaming failures on the ignorance of practitioners rather than the falsity of the art.</summary>

### SECOND PART CHAPTER I.

...the philosophers, however, possessed a higher understanding and were much more diligent in their practical labor. For as Ludovicus Lazarelli <note>Lodovico Lazzarelli (1447–1500) was an Italian poet and Hermeticist who translated works attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> says, in order to recognize the deep secrets of Nature, they often ventured into caves and dwelt in forests and upon mountains. There, with great intellect and sensitivity, they researched the stars to see what power they held, which places on earth were most suitable for metals, which were best for the <term>Materia</term> <note>The "First Matter" or base substance required to begin the alchemical process</note>, and what distinctions existed between them. And for this reason, through their long research, this Divine Work was discovered for their benefit and the benefit of their "children" <note>In alchemical texts, "children" or "sons of the Art" refers to initiated students or faithful followers of the hermetic tradition</note>. For only the Philosophers and their children know and understand the character and <term>Disposition</term> <note>The natural arrangement or "temperament" of elements within a substance</note> of Nature.

Therefore, since so many magnificent Philosophers confirm that this art of <term>Transmutation</term> <note>The transformation of base metals like lead into noble metals like gold</note> can be achieved, and have left behind so many written books, it is unjust and foolish to deny the truth of this art, even if no argument or experience had yet proven or tested it.

Thus Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the art to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> rightly said that there is a great difference between a wise man and an unwise one, and between a blind man and one who sees. Such a judgment also exists between a poor <term>laborant</term> <note>original: "Laboranten"; a practical worker or chemist who performs the physical experiments</note> and an ignorant one. It is therefore concluded from this that this Art is truthful.

## CHAPTER II.

### That not all who believe the Art to be true know how to use it or how to work according to its principles.

There are indeed many who firmly believe that this most noble Art is true. But whether it is truly so, they have not yet experienced through action, nor do they know how to prove it. Some are quite weak in their belief; they agree with the truth and cling to it either because of the many proverbs or the great reputation of the writers. However, they may easily be persuaded to abandon it.

But there is one single thing that easily draws all men to believe such things: namely, the desire for possession and for <term>pleasure</term> <note>original: "wollust"; here meaning a greedy desire for the luxury and wealth that alchemical gold would provide</note>. For pleasure alone makes them eager for it. For that same Ludovicus—

...dovicus Lazzarelli: That men, being devoted to earthly pleasures, desire these same earthly pleasures above all things, and spare no toil or labor to bring them about, according to the verse of <term>Virgil</term> <note>Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BCE), the Roman poet. The quote is from the Aeneid (3.57)</note>:

> O holy hunger for Gold, what do you not compel human hearts to do? <note>original: "Auri sacra fames, quid non mortalia pectora cogis?" In this context, "sacra" is used in the Latin sense of "accursed" or "monstrous," though the German text translates it as "holy" (heiliger).</note>

Since all men generally seek pleasure and wish to live as well and happily as they can, almost all the pleasures of the world can be obtained primarily through money, according to the common proverb: All things are obedient to money. And <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE). However, through the mastery of this Art, very great riches and Medicine for all bodily diseases are promised—namely, true Gold and Silver, and much of it, and moreover without great toil, from which one can mint money through which everything can be obtained.

Therefore, people—those who know and those who do not—easily believe it and desire to test it, and to obtain it through testing. Yet there are few of them who attain the truth of the Art through toil and labor; the primary cause of this has been indicated before: namely, ignorance of the Secrets and negligence in study. There are also two specific causes for this: figurative speech. Regarding this, <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were foundational to later European alchemy</note> says:

> I have considered the books that confirm the Art; however, I found them empty of the foundations and causes that exist in every art, and I found much therein that is not understood, like a transformation—that is, figures or parables. But when I returned to the natural beginnings, I then recognized that the Art was true.

The other cause is the mixing of the true with the false. Regarding this, <term>Arnoldus</term> <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note> says in his *Testament*:

> The Philosophers have set down two ways and methods in their books: one true and one false. They set the true way in obscure words, so that it could be understood by none but the **Sons of Doctrine** <note>original: "Filiis doctrinæ," referring to initiated students or those divinely granted insight</note>; namely, so that the way to do evil would not be shown to the godless. But the false way they have set down in understandable words: and this way has been followed generally by all those who labor in <term>Mercury</term>, in a foreign <term>Sulfur</term>, and in <term>Arsenic</term>, even in the [metallic] bodies themselves, and they have found nothing.

There are, therefore, very many who have labored in this Art, but in vain; for they can neither discover through their own understanding that thing which is suitable for the work, nor can they understand and extract the truth from the opinions of others. For they fail either in the proper **Material**, or in the improper **Operation** and process.

## That it is given only to the Philosophers to recognize and make this Medicine.

# PART TWO CHAPTER IV.

In such a great multitude and variety of things, it is very difficult to recognize which thing is suited to this work and closest to the nature of metals. It is, however, much more difficult to recognize and to know which way of working is most powerful: just as it was harder to recognize from which principles and beginnings the metals are generated, than by what order and how they are perfected; and yet they have discovered both through their skill and investigation.

Of the first, <term>M. Bonus</term> <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist from Ferrara known for his work *The Precious New Pearl*</note> says in chapter 6:
> The knowledge of the Material is no small gift to those who desire to come to the Art. For it is this which the Philosophers sought before all else, so that they might come into the knowledge of the Form.

For every form has its own Material from which it is drawn, without the knowledge of which they would have known nothing in the Art and its operation. Secondly, <term>M. Bonus</term> says in the very same place:
> The Philosophers were endowed with a very subtle understanding and with this sharp-wittedness—by a wonderful, high, and hidden operation, through a suitable and proper <term>Digestion</term> <note>A process of slow, gentle heating intended to mature or "ripen" a substance</note> and cooking—to draw the **Living Silver** <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; common mercury</note> out of the **Arsenic**, which is entirely one thing with the **Common Quicksilver**, so that it may be Coagulated <note>To turn from a liquid to a solid state</note> with itself, just as molten Gold is coagulated by itself by its internal **Sulfur**. For that same **Living Silver** has within it the aforementioned essential and proper Sulfur. For every **Sulfur**, or that which has the nature of **Sulfur**, also has the property to Coagulate the **Living Silver**.

From this, it is understood that the Philosophers had both: namely, a certain and specific Material, and also a certain <term>Magisterium</term> <note>A master-process or "regiment" of specific alchemical steps</note> and rule: from which, and through which, they have truly made the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>, which is the most precious among all its kind.

There is no doubt, however, that many reached this secret with great danger, many errors, and much toil and labor, as <term>Geber</term> <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, often considered the father of chemistry</note> says of himself. Of others, he also says:
> The searching Philosophers have desired this division of **Sulfur**, for they have said that **Arsenic** is the **Sulfur**, or else equal to the **Sulfur**, and not the **Living Silver**. For outwardly it is a **Sulfur**, but in secret it is **Living Silver**, namely when it becomes snow-white through <term>Sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then reverts to a solid again, used for purification</note>; thus they shall exert themselves and labor greatly to research and devise, and often to try in their knowledge, that hidden Material which is in the **Arsenic**. Therefore, the Philosophers have publicly set down **Arsenic** or <term>Orpiment</term> <note>A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral once used as a pigment</note> as the Material of the **Stone**.

If Nature had not made this, then the Art of **Alchemy** would be entirely in vain and useless.

### Part Two, Chapter IV.
B iij

<meta>catchword: who</meta>

To different people, God has also shared various gifts according to the circumstances of time and place, as He saw fit and useful for those to whom He gave them. This is true not only of spiritual gifts, which concern the soul and the virtues, but also of temporal gifts, which belong to the body itself or to external things—such as wealth, honor, health, strength, and the craft of handiwork. But among all other arts, this one [Alchemy] is the most excellent. Firstly, because of its philosophical value, for it is closest to philosophy. Secondly, because of the ease of the work; for one does not need to labor long or hard. Thirdly, because of the immeasurable use and fruit, for countless blessings follow from it.

This **Stone** is also nobler and more miraculous than all others; for this reason, it is not given to everyone. For the best things belong to the minority. I do not tell everyone what it is and how it is made; rather, it is given to very few who know how they ought to do it. For God ordains all things so that they are harmful neither to Him nor to other people. If it were given to the wicked, they could do much harm. If it were given to all the pious, not every one of them would use such a great gift correctly, as the first pious Philosophers did, who applied it to the common good. Therefore, they rightfully received this gift of God, so they had enough for themselves and could share with others.

Therefore <term>Calid</term> <note>Khalid ibn Yazid (d. 704), an Umayyad prince credited as one of the earliest practitioners of alchemy.</note> says: this secret of the praiseworthy God is primarily a sister of philosophy. 
> But it has been inspired by God into the prophets and certain specific, chosen believers. 

And <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the hermetic and alchemical tradition.</note> says right at the beginning: 
> You possess the knowledge of this art only through the inspiration of the one God. 

And <term>Morienus</term> <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit of Jerusalem said to have taught the prince Calid.</note>: 
> The purpose and intent of every person who seeks this Divine Art should mean nothing else than that it is a gift of the highest and greatest God, who reveals it to His servants—blessed be His name. 

Likewise <term>Geber</term> <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), often called the father of chemistry, whose Latinized name was Geber.</note> says: 
> Our art is held in the power of God, who gives it to or withholds it from whomever He wills. 

And <term>Parmenides</term> in the <term>Turba</term> <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential alchemical texts in Latin, presented as a debate between ancient Greek philosophers.</note>: 
> This is a special thing, to which God gives the power. 

And <term>Balgus</term> <note>A philosopher character appearing in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> in the *Turba*: 
> Its governance is greater than can be grasped by reason, unless it be given through the inspiration of God.

Therefore all Philosophers say that it is a gift of God. For whoever knows, makes, or takes it—God grants it to them or withdraws it from them.

## CHAPTER V.

### That the Philosophers have hidden this Stone and its regimen.

The **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists and seekers of natural wisdom.</note> have hidden this most precious **Stone** in two ways: First, by speaking of it only through figures and parables. ### Chapter VI.

### That the **Philosophers' Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> is made from a single thing, and not from many.

Henceforth we wish to examine whether this Stone is simple or composed of many things: And we say that the **Philosophers' Stone**, by the nature of its origin, is a single, simple, divisible thing. For just as it is born of Nature, so it enters into our Mastership alone, without the addition of any other thing that is outside the nature of its forms. And this is confirmed by all the Philosophers.

For **Mundus** <note>A speaker often featured in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an early Latin alchemical text.</note> says in the **Assembly of the Philosophers**: <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, which presents a debate between various pre-Socratic philosophers.</note> You should not concern yourselves with a multitude of compositions, nor with those things which the Philosophers have set down in their books. For the secret of truth is a single nature; and what it has hidden in its belly is not seen, nor is it recognized, except by the wise alone. And in the **Book of Saturn**: This science is nothing other than a perfect inspiration from God: For the entire Mastership consists only in a single thing, which is called **Adrop**. <term>Adrop: A technical term in alchemy, often referring to the "Lead of the Philosophers" or the raw material of the Stone.</term> Likewise **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who supposedly taught the Art to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says in **The Book of Crates**: <note>original: "Castrensi"</note> The first and foremost substance and matter of this thing is one; it is from one, with him it becomes one, nor is anything else added to it or taken from it. And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says: Just as all things come from one thing: So also is this Mastership made from a single matter and substance. **Morienus**: There are many names for the single root: But you will find only a single root (which is the essence and substance of this Mastership) without any other matter. **Senior** <note>Referring to Senior Zadith, the Latinized name of the 10th-century alchemist Ibn Umail.</note>: One nature joins the others together; Nature rejoices in her nature, and yet it is only a single nature, one kind, one substance, one essence. Likewise **Alphidius** in the **Assembly**: It is one stone, one nature, one composition, and one vessel, to make the **White** and the **Red** <note>Referring to the Albedo (white) and Rubedo (red) stages of the Great Work, representing the two final degrees of the Stone's perfection.</note> at the same time. Therefore the **Rosary** <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, the source text the author is expanding upon.</note> concludes: A seeker of this Art must be of a constant will in the work, so that he does not attempt now this, then that, for our Art does not consist in a multitude of things. For there is only one Stone, one single correct way, one medicine, to which nothing external is added nor anything taken away, except only that one...

## CHAPTER VII.
### That our singular Stone contains many things within itself.

<margin>B.</margin>

## Chapter VI.

# That the Philosophers' Stone is made from a single thing, and not from many.

Henceforth we shall examine whether this Stone is simple, or composed of many things. We say that the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>Lapis Philosophorum: The ultimate goal of alchemy, believed to be a substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</term> is, by the nature of its origin, a single, simple, and yet divisible thing. For just as it is born of Nature, so it enters alone into our **Mastership** <note>original: "Meisterschafft"; referring to the alchemical process or the Great Work.</note> without the addition of any other thing that is outside the nature of its forms. And this is confirmed by all the Philosophers.

For **Mundus** <note>A speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says in the **Assembly**: <note>original: "Turba"; The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts.</note> You should not trouble yourselves with the multiplicity of the composition, nor with those things which the Philosophers have set down in their books. For the secret of truth is a single Nature; and that which it has hidden in its belly is not seen, nor is it recognized, except by the Wise alone. And in the **Book of Saturn**: This science is nothing other than a perfect inspiration from God: for the entire Mastership consists only in a single thing, which is called **Adrop**. <term>Adrop: A technical term often used by alchemists to refer to "the body," lead, or the raw starting material of the Stone.</term> Likewise, **Morienus of Castre** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says: The first and most noble substance and matter of this thing is singular; and from it is one, and with it becomes one, nor is anything else added to it or taken away from it. And **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical father of alchemy.</note> says: Just as all things come forth from one thing, so also is this Mastership made from a single matter and substance. Morienus: There are many names for this single root: but you will find only one root (which is the essence and substance of this Mastership) without any [other] matter. **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century Arabic alchemist known as "Senior" in the Latin West.</note>: One nature joins the others together; Nature rejoices in her own nature, and yet it is but a single nature, one kind, one substance, one essence. Likewise, **Alphidius** in the Assembly: It is one Stone, one nature, one composition, and one vessel, to make the **White and the Red** at the same time. <note>The "White" and "Red" refer to the two final stages of the Stone's perfection: the White Elixir for silver and the Red Elixir for gold.</note> Therefore, the **Rosary** <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, the source text being compiled here.</note> concludes: A seeker of this Art must be of a steady will in the Work, so that he does not attempt now this and then quickly another thing; for our Art does not consist in a multiplicity of things. For there is only one Stone, one single correct path, one **Medicine**, <term>Medicine: Alchemists often called the Stone a "Medicine" because it was thought to "cure" base metals of their "impurities" and "illness" to make them gold.</term> to which nothing external is added, nor is anything taken away, except only that the...

## CHAPTER VII.

### That our single Stone comprises many things.

<margin>Note well.</margin>
**A**lthough our Stone is single in its essence and nature, it is nevertheless composed of many things which bring about its perfection. This is true not only in its external and hidden aspects—as is the case with many other things—but also in the distinctness of its manifest parts. For one thing contains or joins together, but two things make a **Medicine** <term>Medicin: In alchemy, this refers to the Elixir or the Stone itself, capable of "curing" base metals of their imperfections or "illness."</term>. Therefore, three things are contained within one body, as a Philosopher says. **Hercules** in **Morienus Castrensis** <note>Morienus Romanus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist; "Castrensis" likely refers to his supposed residence in a hermitage or camp.</note>: This **Mastership** <note>original: "Meisterschafft"; the alchemical process or "Great Work."</note> springs from a single root, which is thereafter extended into many things, and returns again into one thing.

For the correct weight and **Proportion** <note>original: "Proportion"; the specific ratio of ingredients.</note> is entirely unknown to the human understanding; and thereafter cook them into a thick pulp, which nonetheless seems worthless. ### SECOND PART, CHAPTER VII.

Four things come from one, from which all things have their origin. Therefore, this Mastery <term>Meisterschafft: the Great Work of alchemy or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> is made from a single substance and material. And although four elements are united and joined together in a single body, and spread through the whole **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note>, they nonetheless have an unequal color and governance. And **Astanus** <note>Likely referring to Ostanes, a legendary alchemist and sage of the Persian tradition</note> says: The four elements—namely, heat and moisture, dryness and cold—flow from a single spring. And these four **Elements** <note>original: *Elementa*</note> are very well proportioned in this Stone’s hidden **Body** <note>original: *Corpore*</note>, and are entirely similar to the **Complexion** <term>Complexion: the specific balance of the four humors or elements that determines a person's physical and mental character</term> of man. Therefore, in the **Universal Way** <note>original: *Via universali*</note> it is said: In this thing are four **Elements** <note>original: *Elementa*</note>, most excellently proportioned by Nature: and in the same are the forming and the fixed, the tinting <term>tingierende: the power to permeate and transform the color and nature of a substance</term> and the colored, the male and the female joined together: and in the work, the two **Seeds** <note>original: *Spermata*</note> must not rest until they are mixed. Even in such an order does the Stone comprise the four **Elements**, and this is the reason why the **Philosophers** <note>original: *Philosophi*</note> have called this Art an Egg. Yet they do not simply call it an egg, as **Lilium** <note>referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae* or similar alchemical text</note> says, but add something to it. For they call it the **Philosophers' Egg** <note>original: *Ovum Philosophorum*</note> because of the similarity it has with an egg. # CHAPTER VIII.
## That the Stone is both Lowly and Precious.

<margin>
Note:
This is also very remarkable
</margin>

**N**ow that we have spoken of the Stone and its composition, we must henceforth also examine its lowliness as well as its preciousness.
Regarding its worthlessness, **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: Everything that is bought at a high price is of no use for this work and will be found worthless. And **Haly** <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an Arab astrologer and alchemist</note> says: This Stone is found among the poor and the rich, with the one who walks and the one who sits. And in the **Book of Saturn**: Everyone knows the Stone; even the blind know it and could have it.
Regarding its preciousness, **Rafis** <note>Rhazes (al-Razi), a Persian polymath and physician</note> says in the *Book of Words*: Praise be to Him who created the most precious thing out of the most lowly. And the **Lilium** <note>The *Lilium Intelligentiae*, an alchemical text</note>, as **Zeno** says: This stone is openly bought for a small sum of money; if the sellers knew what it was, they would keep it in their hands and by no means sell it. Regarding both aspects, **Rafis** says: This art is to be preferred far above others, for in it there is little expense, little effort and labor, a short time, great profit, a desired certainty, and a generosity followed by joy. And it is a Stone, and yet not a Stone, lowly and precious, despised and chosen; it has but one name, and yet many names. This very Stone is also the most precious of all, for without it Nature works nothing. But how can a thing be both lowly and precious at the same time? Answer: When it is considered in itself, it is lowly, for it is often thrown upon the dunghill <note>The "dunghill" (stercus) is a frequent alchemical metaphor for the raw, unrefined matter of the Stone, which most people overlook</note> and bought for little money. But when one considers its effect and operation, it is most precious of all, for from it is made the most noble **Elixir**. And thus all metals are in it **potentially** <note>original: *potestate*</note>, and especially gold, which is the most precious of all. And this is in two ways: First, in **remote potential** <note>original: *Potentia remota*; a philosophical term for a capacity that requires several steps to be realized</note>, when one considers its essence before preparation; afterward, in **most immediate potential** <note>original: *potentia propinquissima*; a state where the matter is ready to transform into the final form</note>, when it is considered after perfection and completion. Therefore Nature, according to the opinion of **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, author of the *Precious Pearl*</note>, generates from the **being in potential** <note>original: *Ente in potentia*</note> a **being in actuality and in an instant** <note>original: *Ens actu & in instanti*</note>, as **Aristotle** says in **Book 9 of the Metaphysics**. Yet all suitable dispositions and orders must precede this, which make the matter fit to take a form upon itself; and according to how the matter is disposed in various ways, it also receives one form after another. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the generation of the Stone from Chapter VIII. ### SECOND PART, CHAPTER VIII.

[Genera]tion and birth come from the immediate beginnings, as is evident from the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Metaphysicorum"; a reference to Aristotle’s work on the nature of being and substance</note>. Just as the two spirits of Nature—namely Sulfur and Mercury—are bodies in potential <note>original: "potestate"; meaning they have the inherent capacity to become solid matter but have not yet done so</note>, for they are the principles and elements of metals; and conversely, they are so materially and formally <note>original: "Materialiter vnd Formaliter"; referring to the physical "stuff" and the essential "blueprint" of the metal</note>, as is shown by the appearance of their ores.

For out of these spirits alone does Nature make bodies in actuality <note>original: "Actu"; the realized, physical state of an object</note>, and vice versa. Not that she mixes the bodies with spirits so that the spirits are converted into the bodies. Thus, Art <note>In this context, "Art" refers to the skilled practice of alchemy</note> also generates an Elixir from the immediate principles and beginnings, out of which gold is generated. For the Elixir is the immediate form of gold. Or, the principles of gold are only two spirits, namely Sulfur and Mercury <note>The "Sulfur and Mercury" of the alchemists were not the common chemicals, but philosophical principles representing the "soul" and "spirit" of metals</note>. Likewise, Nature makes stable bodies—namely gold—solely out of these same spirits without the addition of any other body. This happens so that such spirits, through suitable decoction <note>The alchemical process of heating a substance in a fluid</note>, take upon themselves the property, nature, and essence of a body, and become stable out of their own selves alone. Therefore, Art also makes a stable Elixir in the fire solely out of these same spirits.

And just as the mineral spirits are not common, but changed, so too are the spirits of Art. And just as Nature makes bodies in actuality only out of those spirits that are bodies in potential, so also should Art do. And just as Nature does not mix foreign things into her principles—for that would hinder the generation—so also should Art. And just as Nature has two principles—one which has the nature of an active force <note>original: "wirckenden"</note> and the other the nature of matter or the passive force <note>original: "leidenten"</note>—so also does Art. And just as Nature sets these principles together at once in a certain measure and weight, so also should Art do. However, because Art cannot know the proper weight, she must, as a servant, take such things as they have already been put together by Nature. Therefore, a single material shall be weighed out by Nature in which Art shall work, and that same material is enough.

From which it follows of necessity that all the distinctions found in mineral gold must also be in the Stone <note>original: "Lapide"</note> and Elixir in potential. And these same things become manifest in the gold, which happens through the Elixir in actuality: namely, that it be entirely heavy, citron-red <note>A deep, golden-orange color prized by alchemists</note>, most brilliantly shining, incombustible, perfectly tempered, and a great medicine. From all of this, it is further concluded that the two spirits—namely Sulfur and Mercury—alone are the beginnings and matter of the Me[tals]...

# ROSARII NOVI

minerals, and are themselves **metals in potential**. <note>original: "Metalla potestate"; referring to the Aristotelian idea that matter has the inherent "power" or capacity to take a specific form before it actually becomes that form</note> Therefore Art <note>In alchemical texts, "Art" refers to the labor and skill of the alchemist</note> also makes an **Elixir** out of these same **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritibus"</note> alone, or from those mixed by Nature, which is gold in **potential**: provided that a proper preparation precedes it. And indeed, these **spirits** are for themselves alone and with themselves a **body in potential**. Thus now comes the **Mercurial spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus Mercurialis"</note>, which is the **subject** <note>original: "Subjectum"; the underlying substance or raw material</note> of Nature, and the spirit which is entirely equal to it is the **subject** of Art, once it is brought to light by the artful **sublimation** <note>original: "Sublimation"; a process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then re-solidifies, used here as a metaphor for purification</note> from its impurity through a suitable fire. And then it is a simple, volatile **spirit**, which the **philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophi"</note> have known before, and it is a **body in the most immediate potential**. <note>original: "Corpus in potestate propinquissima"</note> Therefore we must make it perfect without the addition of any other external thing, and transform it into an essential **body** so that it may be a stable **Elixir**, entirely red like blood, and then it is the **Solar body of the philosophers** <note>original: "Corpus solare Philosophorum"; gold is associated with the Sun (Sol), so this is the "Gold of the Sages"</note> and an everlasting **tincture**, and that is the gold, lead, and ore **of the philosophers**. Of which **Milvesindus** <note>An authority often cited in the "Rosarium" corpus, likely representing a medieval alchemical tradition</note> says: Our ore does not tinge or color unless it is first made volatile. And this is the **Sulphur of the philosophers**, and their hidden gold in the **living mercury of the philosophers**. <note>original: "Mercurio vivo Philosophorum"</note>

From this it is evident that not only are the bodies of metals made from their spirits: but the birth of almost all minerals is from their own **vapors** <note>original: "Vaporibus"</note> and fumes, whether they be simple or compounded. All of these **vapors** are of the nature and genus of spirits, for they fly from the heat: yet at the end of the **digestion** <note>original: "Digestion"; the process of slow, constant heating to mature a substance</note> and cooking, they are **fixed** <note>original: "figiert"; "fixation" in alchemy means making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates under heat</note> and made stable by a penetrating cold. And they are made stable by themselves with their hidden bodies, which they contain in **potential** <note>original: "Potestate"</note>, without any addition of an external **body**, whatever it may be. From this, the preciousness of the Stone is evident: yet we wish to

# C H A P T E R IX.

## That this Stone has only one proper name, and yet is called by many names.

Just as this blessed Stone is a single thing, so it is also called by only one name, namely *Trifonis* <note>original: "Trifonis"; likely a reference to the "three-fold" nature of the stone—Spirit, Soul, and Body—or a corruption of a Greek term for the "Triple-natured"</note>: nevertheless, it is called by nearly countless names, and by the names of all things. And this multitude of names comes from two kinds of people: First, from the **Philosophers** <note>In alchemy, "Philosophers" refers to the legendary practitioners and authors of alchemical secrets, such as Hermes or Aristotle</note>. Hence **Bonellus** in the **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: To this thing, many names are given because of the various colors that appear during the **Operation** <note>the technical process of the alchemical work</note>. The same **Bonellus** says: The envious <note>original: "neidigen"; a standard term for alchemists who intentionally hid their secrets from the "unworthy" or "uninitiated"</note> have created many names so that they might lead their successors astray, as **Hermogenus** says. The Philosophers, however, call this Stone by various names and in various ways. Sometimes by the name of a stone, soon an animal, an ore, or tin, iron, or lead; yes, they have called it by the names of all bodies; sometimes a spirit, then a body, an egg, soon with the names of all sorts of things, etc. And they have done such for three reasons.

First, because of the colors that appear in the working, and which indicate the many **Effects** <note>original: "Effecta"; the results or transformations</note> and changes. For in its **Operation**, all the colors in the world that can be imagined are seen. And therefore, because of the manifold colors that appear in the **Operation**, they have given the same thing various names. Hence **Morienus** <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: The wise seek this **Mastery** <note>original: "Magisterium"; the goal of the alchemical process</note> earnestly, and find it, love it, and adorn it: But the fools laugh at it and hold it for nothing. For they do not know what it is, and there are many names with which the wise have called it in their places: Which is a **Sperm** <note>original: "Sperma"; used here to mean a biological seed or foundational essence</note> or seed, which if it is changed, is turned into blood, and finally becomes hard, and like a chewed piece of flesh <note>This "chewed flesh" description refers to a specific stage of the work called coagulation, where the matter thickens</note>. There are also many other names, for all of which there is only a single root; rather, because of the manifold colors, powers, and virtues, they have also given it various names.

Then <note>meaning the second reason</note>, because it comprises so many things within itself. For this Stone is composed of all four **Elements** <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, as was said above. Therefore they have [called it] by the name of every thing which [is composed] of the Ele-

## C H A P T E R X.

### That many who seek the Stone cannot find it, but instead go astray.

Many of you, who read the books of the **Philosophers** and believe that the **Philosophers' Stone** can be made, seek and find nothing; you labor and err, and lose both your life and your goods over it. Of which thing there are two causes.

The first is the hiding of its own name. For they do not simply call it by its own name, but add something to it. Hence the **Lily** says: Kings seek this stone and do not find it, except for a very few—namely, those to whom God reveals it. For although the **Philosophers** sometimes [call] this thing by its right [name]...

...named them, yet they always add something fictional so that it might not be recognized.

The second reason is the multitude of varied names. Thus **Ernech** <note>A variant name often associated with Hermes Trismegistus or Enoch in alchemical literature</note> in **Morienus** says: Nothing else has led those seeking the **Masterpiece** <note>original: *Magisterii*; the "Great Work" of alchemy</note> into error more than the sheer quantity and variety of names. And because they have changed the names during a single preparation, just as they have changed the many colors. Therefore, when they read through the books and find many different names, they get a false idea of the **Material of the Stone**, and each person gets a different one, according to how their own thoughts and fantasies—rather than natural reason—incite them.

This is why one person labors in this **Material** and another in that one; yet none of them work in the suitable material, of which there are many kinds. In this number, there have been many noble men, well-experienced in **Philosophy** <note>In this context, meaning "Natural Philosophy" or the precursor to modern science</note>, who considered the **Principles** <note>original: *Principia*; the fundamental building blocks of matter</note> of nature **universally** and in general, but did not observe the "proximate" or immediate nature. And just as they only considered **particular generation** <note>original: *Particularem generationem*; the specific process by which a specific thing is born or created</note> and judged the birth of metals falsely, so too did they act in the beginnings of the Art and its various effects. Thus, they have always remained in **sophistry** <note>deceptive or false reasoning</note> and have never reached the perfection of the Stone of which the Philosophers speak.

Some, however, have worked in the true beginnings of Nature and the Art, but they were entirely ignorant of the correct **Regimen** <note>original: *Regiment*; the specific sequence of operations, heat levels, and timing required</note> of the Art. Therefore, they erred no less than the others.

Since many well recognize that the **Elixir** is the **form of Gold** <note>original: *forma Auri*</note> and **Silver** <note>original: *Argenti*</note> which informs and transforms the **imperfect metals**, they have believed that the Elixir must be made from the **Principles of the metals**. The **Principles** of the metals, however, are **Sulfur** and **Mercury**. From this, they concluded that the **Stone of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Lapis Philosophorum*</note> is made either from one of these or from both together; for the Philosophers have called the Stone by those very names.

Some, however, have also added **Arsenic** to this; some have added **Marcasite** <note>A common iron sulfide mineral</note> or **Calamine** <note>original: *Galmey*; an ore used in making brass</note> or **Antimony** or other minerals, and labored therein.

Others have applied their work to **animal** and **vegetable** things; and they have all been brought to shame because of a double lack: namely, of the suitable Material and the proper **Operation**. For they have not correctly considered the specific and proximate **Principles**, of which there are three: namely, **Quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentum vivum*; literally "living silver"</note> and **Sulfur**, though transformed, and the proper **measure and proportion** mixed by Nature; and the mine- <note>The text ends mid-word: "mine-", likely referring to minerals (German: *mineralische* or *mineralien*)</note>

...natural boiling heat and the virtue <note>The "virtue" refers to the inherent power or specific quality</note> of the place, which is the beginning of **Generation** <term>Generation: the natural process by which metals "grow" in the earth</term>, impressed upon the **Heavenly Bodies**: each of which for itself introduces an inequality in the birth of **Metals** <note>original: *Metalla*</note>: But much more so all together. From the first, follows the opposition of the **Elements** or rather of the elemental things, from which the metals are generated. Thus, these same **Qualities** of the elements are found in simple things as well as in those that are composed.

Therefore, the metals unite with one another in their common **Passions** <note>original: *Passionibus*; here meaning the ways they are acted upon or their shared characteristics</note>, for they only desire a final form. Rather, a third nature, mixed in the right **measure** <note>original: *mensur*</note>, is born from them: Otherwise, Nature could not bring them to one place to fulfill generation. For neither the nature of minerals nor of plants has those same **local motions** <note>original: *Motus locales*; the ability to move from one place to another independently</note> for generation.

But **Art** <note>Alchemy was known as "The Art," the human practice of perfecting nature</note> has both of these in division and joining. Therefore, this third nature must have a common nature in itself, which is changed from the nature of those things which compose it: and which comes from its manifold mixtures and digestion: And in this third nature is the **Mineral** virtue <note>original: *tugent Mineralis*</note> to generate a **Compound** <note>original: *Compositum*</note>.

### SECOND PART, CHAPTER 10.

...for the **Matter**. And such things certainly do not remain under the same form as the **Components** <note>original: *Componentia*</note> or the constituent things were in their first composition. Furthermore, through their mutual acting and suffering <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "acting and suffering" refers to the interaction between active and passive forces</note>, they can be cooked and changed from one form to another, until they reach the final form and **Perfection**, which is the form of **Gold**. And then the **Agent** <term>Agent: the active principle or force that causes change in a substance</term> or the acting power is separated from the **Matter**. Such cooking and **digestion** <term>Digestion: a slow, maturing heat used to ripen or "perfect" a substance</term> occurs in the **Generation** of **Metals**, which **Matter** is mixed from two **Principles** in the mines <note>original: *Mineren*</note>, namely **Sulfur** and **Mercury**. It does not remain in the form it held in its first composition, but one constantly acts and suffers upon the other until a new form is born—namely, an incomplete metal. At that stage, the **Agent** or acting power is not yet separated from the **Matter**. However, if the cooking continues to the very end—that is, until the **Agent** is entirely separated from the **Matter**—then a new form is born, namely that of a perfect metal, which is **Gold**.

From this, it is obvious that all minerals are composed of their **Elements**, mixed in a determined quantity and measure. Thus, among these mixable things, one is not earlier or slower than the other; rather, the composition of the simple and the compound occurs simultaneously and at once, and vice versa, etc. This also occurs in the generation of **Milk**, which is composed of three substances, namely **Cheese**, **Butter**, and **Whey** <note>original: *Milchraum*; likely referring to the watery serum or cream of the milk</note>, and their generation occurs simultaneously with the milk itself.

From this, it is concluded that because the **Metals** are composed solely of two things—namely **Sulfur** and **Mercury**—just as their ores are, the **Art** <note>Alchemy was frequently referred to simply as "The Art"</note> should follow **Nature** entirely. It is therefore necessary that one strives to give birth to an **Elixir** from those very same **Principles**, or those entirely identical to those from which Nature proceeds, and that one observes that same weight. There, the hour of birth is noted and recognized.

From this, it is obvious that those who have labored with **Sulfur** alone have toiled in vain. Firstly, because no matter how much the **Sulfur** is purified through **Sublimation** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term>, it can nevertheless never be of the same composition and substance as **Gold**. Nor can it be taken as a **Matter**, for no **Agent** or acting power would be set in place of the **Matter**. Furthermore, because **Sulfur** alone has no **Matter** upon which it may act through constant cooking, from which it might finally extract a form **out of the potential of matter** <note>original: *de potentia materiæ*</note>. For if this could happen, it would leave...

<meta>This page continues the critique of various alchemical methods, building on the previous discussion of how Nature "cooks" metals from Sulfur and Mercury. The text now explains why certain human attempts to replicate this process fail.</meta>

# THE NEW ROSARY
<meta>catchword: dert. (likely "fordert" / "requires")</meta>

...to consider / that such should primarily happen in the **Mineral** <term>Minera: the raw ore or natural state of a substance in the earth</term> in which it would be brought to the perfection of the **Medicine** <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" refers to the transformative substance, such as the Philosopher's Stone, that "heals" base metals into gold</note>. And after it has mixed itself with **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>, it is quickly coagulated into a metal, which however does not happen.

Thirdly, because **Sulfur** <term>Sulphur: the active, combustible, and masculine principle in alchemy</term> cannot be made stable unless one **calcinates** <term>Calcination: the process of reducing a substance to a dry powder through intense heat</term> it, and it cannot be calcinated otherwise than through **Sublimation** <term>Sublimation: heating a substance until it becomes vapor, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</term>. Both of these are very difficult to achieve because sulfur is so combustible. But it is much harder to **tinge** <term>Tinge: the act of changing the color and nature of a metal using an alchemical tincture</term> it with a perfect medicine—and entirely impossible to do so with a shining one, as the **Elixir** <term>Elixir: the ultimate goal of the work, used for transformation and healing</term> requires.

Others, however, who labor only in **Quicksilver** <term>Argento vivo: literally "living silver," the common term for mercury</term>, err even more—as Aldimarus <note>Possibly a reference to a medieval alchemical authority or a corruption of a name like Adfar</note> says—who first sublimate it and thereafter **fix** <note>To "fix" a substance means to make a volatile material solid and resistant to fire</note> it with gentle fire for eighty days until it receives a metallic flow. But this medicine is in vain, for it cannot be made perfect from a suffering matter <note>referring to Mercury as the passive, "suffering" principle</note> alone without an active **Sulfur**. Since **Mercury** also has much impurity and cannot digest or cook its own coarseness by itself.

Others have attempted to make the **Stone** <term>Lapidem: the Philosopher's Stone</term> from **Mercury** and **Sulfur** mixed together at the same time, which is no less impossible. For firstly, even if each were digested and cooked on its own, they could still not achieve the purpose of Nature. Secondly, because no one can know what proportion and measure are necessary, both in minerals and in metals. Thirdly, because each for itself requires a heavy **Preparation** <note>original: *Praeparation*</note> and readiness; they will be much heavier to prepare if they are both mixed together.

Others labor only in **Gold**: but they also do not act according to the opinion of the **Philosophers** <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the collective wisdom of ancient and medieval alchemical masters</note>. Firstly, because even if its Sulfur could tinge its **Quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum: Mercury</term> from whose **Power** <note>original: *Potentia*</note> it was extracted, it is still not enough to transform another gold, or to increase or multiply its **tincture**, because its tincture is already at the final degree in the metals. Secondly, the work of the Philosophers does not require great expense—specifically for those who have researched the right way of Nature and the proper regime. Of this **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: You need not squander your goods, for you will come to perfect mastery with little expense if you know the **Principles** <note>original: *Principia*</note> of the Art (which we, however, teach). Gold, however, is expensive, and thus the poor would be forced to abandon this magnificent work. And since it happens that an artist oftentimes errs, a poor man could not repeat the work and start anew, as this Art requires.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the difficulties of the alchemical work, transitioning from the physical requirements to the financial and material pitfalls that trap the inexperienced or the poor.</meta>

### SECOND PART, CHAPTER X.

...requires <note>original: "dert," likely the end of "erfordert" (requires)</note>. And thus, those who approach this operation of the Art and a full understanding could, because of great poverty, neither labor nor accomplish anything. Regarding these, **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in 8th-century chemistry/alchemy</note> says: That such people are oppressed by poverty and, due to a lack of funding <note>original: "verlags," meaning financial backing or outlay</note>, are forced to set aside such a noble work.

Therefore, the poor are not hindered in the preparation of the **Stone** <term>Lapis: the Philosopher's Stone</term>, but it depends entirely on the attendance <note>original: "auſſwarten," referring to the constant tending of the alchemical furnace over long periods</note>. (This is entirely true; and whoever knows such Art for this reason does not quickly go to great Lords to perform it for them. Therefore **Zacharius** <note>Denis Zachaire, a 16th-century French alchemist</note> says that they are deceivers who want to make the **Stone** at another's expense, since the wise are able to make it without the help of strange men.) There must, therefore, from the beginning of the operation, be a single humble Material of the Art, in which the virtue of a body, spirit, and soul is equal to the mineral material.

Others, however, labor with **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>, ore, and the **Ferment of Gold** <note>original: *Fermento Solis*, literally "Ferment of the Sun"</note> or **Silver** <note>original: *Lunae*, "of the Moon"</note>, which they take because the Philosophers often call the **Stone** an ore. But they are deceived. Firstly, because the Philosophers speak of the "ore of the Philosophers," which is also called our gold or **Physical Gold** <note>original: *Aurum Physicum*</note>; likewise Iron and Lead. Secondly, because the ore has much impure sulfurousness in it, which spoils the **Medicine** <note>The transformative alchemical substance</note>, and which can hardly, or not at all, be removed during purification. Such a **Sulfur** <note>original: *Sulphur*</note>, however, is not of the essence and being of Gold. Likewise, Gold is of entirely shining and purest natures, and its parts are of a single substance and not of a dissimilar nature. Thirdly, even if the **Ferment of Gold** <note>original: *Fermentum auri*</note> is mixed in, the gold cannot perfect the ore in its virtue as much as it is diminished in its own virtue by that same ore. In the same way, this can be said of all those who labor in other metals and exert themselves in vain, finding either nothing or very little after the long toil and labor they have endured. Therefore, as **Arnoldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a prominent 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says in his *Testament*, such operations are very long, tedious, dangerous, and of great expense; at times the entire work is also ruined because of a single deficiency. And even if one begins correctly, they either give it up entirely or otherwise become negligent regarding it. Therefore, even if the **Stone** could be made from the metals, it is more advisable to leave the work alone than to begin it.

Several also labor with **Salts** <note>original: *Salibus*</note>, **Vitriols** <note>original: *Atramentis*, literally "inks" or black metallic sulfates</note>, and **Alums** <note>original: *Aluminibus*</note>, and dissolve **Gold** <note>original: *Solem*, "the Sun"</note>, **Silver** <note>original: *Lunam*, "the Moon"</note>, or other metals with them, and there—
