From which it is to be concluded that the Philosophers, when they speak of the **Stone** <term>Lapis: the Philosopher's Stone</term>, have used the names of all these things and many other names, and according to their intentions, they have not lied. For under these figures and metaphors they have told the truth; and yet the unwise have taken such significant things literally, as they sound, labored in them, and deceived both themselves and others. Thus, they have not come to the knowledge of the **Stone**, nor have they even fully approached it; instead, they have always produced only **sophistical things** <note>meaning counterfeits or deceptive imitations</note>. For acting according to the literal meaning of the letter is a waste of wealth, as it is written in the **Book of Saturn**.

## CHAPTER XI.

### What properties the Stone has, and how it may be recognized.

<margin>Note:</margin> Although the **Philosopher's Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> cannot be easily recognized, because the Philosophers call it by the names of other things and obscure it with many terms, while keeping its own name secret; nevertheless, if one reads their books faithfully and diligently, he will find what he seeks through the inspiration of God.

There are, however, two things that are useful for finding the **Stone** with its **Mastery** <term>Magisterio: the skillful process or "Magistery" of creating the Stone</term>. The first is reading with diligent reflection, as the **Rosary** <note>referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> says:

> Whoever wishes to be lazy in reading the books cannot be ready or prepared in the preparation of the things.

For one book explains the other, and one speech clarifies the other; for what is omitted in one is fulfilled in another. Therefore, whatever mind refuses to toil in **Theory** <note>original: "Theorica"</note> and reflection will also not easily be able to accustom itself to the **Practice** <note>original: "Practic"</note> and the actual work. And in the **Lily** <note>referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae*</note> it is said:

> Whoever desires to come to our Art sooner, let him not look at our books, for they bring a person great burden and difficulty before they are understood by the reader, even if they have read our books once, twice, or three times.

Secondly, there also belongs to this an honest faithfulness with promised prayer to God. Therefore, the **Lily** says:

> Whoever bows his back to read our books and applies himself to them, and is not entangled with vain fantasies and thoughts, and prays to the Lord, he will [receive] in the Kingdom...

...govern unceasingly until he dies. Likewise: If, out of our speech, or those things which should be said, one is unable to come to the knowledge of our **Stone** due to his own darkened understanding: let him not blame the Sages but himself. For if he seeks and remains ignorant, let him know that God has hidden the truth from him. For if God Himself knew a faithful heart within him, He would certainly grant him the truth, as *Diomedes* <note>Diomedes Grammaticus, though often cited generally as an authority in such texts</note> says. Therefore, everyone should also hide this **Stone**, and especially its **regimen** <term>regiment: the specific sequence of operations or the "rule" for the alchemical process</term>, so that it does not fall into the hands of enemies, for then we would be a cause of their wickedness, for which we would deserve to be punished by God. But God alone can communicate it out of grace to whomever He wills. For He cannot be unjust or unwise; rather, He knows perfectly what is useful for mankind or not.

Therefore, the following should abstain from this blessed Art: warriors, lechers, those who pursue feminine pleasures, the vice-ridden, tyrants, the vengeful, the covetous, the greedy, murderers, and common folk. But as a good *Philosopher* says:

> Let Codrus, a lover of his country's piety, come here,
> And whoever worships **GOD** and the holy stars.
<note>original Latin: "Huc veniat patriæ Codrus pietatis amator, Et quicunque DEUM & sydera sancta colit." Codrus was a legendary king of Athens who sacrificed himself for his people, epitomizing the selfless character required here.</note>

For this holy and golden virtue is hidden from the godless. Therefore, this **Stone**, which has been so diligently hidden by the *Philosophers*, is not easily found. For it transforms many other **metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note>, whether it be found in the true or the sophistical <note>meaning deceptive, counterfeit, or merely based on surface logic</note> manner. Yet it is found by those to whom God Himself grants it, and who pay attention to the understanding of the words, and not just to the literal letters.

This **Stone** is called an **ore** <note>original: "Erz"</note> by the *Philosophers* through metaphor, and yet it is no ore, and yet it is the ore of the Philosophers. Therefore *Eximenes* says in the *Turba* <note>referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the earliest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</note>: You experienced ones should all know that no true **tincture** <term>tincture: the potent substance or "dye" that penetrates and transforms base metals into gold</term> can be made, except alone from our ore. And this must be understood according to the *Lilio* <note>likely referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae* or "Lily of Alchemy," a text often attributed to Raymond Lull</note>, when our composition is perfect and transformed into an **Elixir**. This ore has a Body, Soul, and Spirit; and out of it a **Water** is made, as is evident through the following sayings in the *Lilio*.

# THE NEW ROSARY

When the ore is made white and then also made red, we call it Gold.

It is also called a Lead. Socrates says in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers) is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>:
> You should know that without the Lead no tincture can be made, because it possesses the virtue <note>original: "Tugent"; here meaning the inherent power or efficacy</note>.

Democritus:
> Cook our lead until it becomes red.

And it is called a lead because it is Silver on the outside, but in secret it is Gold; and because it becomes red when it is calcined <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term>.

It is also called <term>Magnesia</term> <note>Magnesia in alchemy refers not to the modern element magnesium, but to the "primal matter" or a mysterious substance that draws the spirit to the body</note> by the envious, for in it is the greatest secret, as Basen says in the *Turba*. But there are also other names that express its nature, though from a distance. There are also some that express and indicate what the <term>Lapis</term> <note>Lapis is Latin for "Stone," the goal of the alchemical work</note> is, primarily because this thing is composed of Soul and Body. Therefore Amigantus says in the *Turba*:
> Our ore has body and soul like a human being.

And just as the respiration and breathing of humans comes from the Air: so our thing is breathed upon by moisture; and for this reason it is called a Human by some. Therefore Raymundus Massiliensis <note>Raimundus of Marseilles, a 12th-century astronomer and translator</note> says:
> The stone which man has taken into himself is that which is superfluous in him in the Spring.

Therefore it is a living creature <note>original: "thier," literally animal/beast</note> which makes the bodies strong. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>:
> The stone is in a thing that has a soul and is spiritual.

Therefore Aristotle says in the book *On the Secret of Secrets* <note>original: "de Secretis Secretorum," a popular medieval pseudo-Aristotelian treatise</note>: That the <term>Stone</term> is Mineral, Vegetable, and Animal. For it has the properties of these things within itself. Therefore one says: Let us thank God, who has refused to give us feathers and wings, and has given us something better.

Since the <term>Stone</term> is now composed of a Body, it cannot do without the Spirit and the Soul, for the Spirit is the bond between the Body and the Soul. Therefore it is also said that it is composed of three things, namely Soul, Spirit, and Body, as was said above. Therefore Johan. Tebit <note>likely referring to Thabit ibn Qurra, a famous astronomer and mathematician</note> says:
> Our Stone is made of three things and is given to no one except through the inspiration of God.

Secondly, it is also called a Philosophers' Egg, because of the similarity it has with the egg, as *Lilium* <note>The "Lilium" or "Lily of Alchemy," a common title for alchemical treatises</note> says, and the aforementioned Johan. Tebit. Note that the truth consists in only three things, from which a true Composition and a perfect <term>Elixir</term> is made, namely from the Lunar Stone, from the Solar Stone, and from the Stone of Mercury <note>original: "ex Lapide Lunari, ex Lapide Solari, & ex Lapide Mercurii"</note>, which comprises both natures, namely the white and the red. Likewise another says: whoever knows how to tincture the <term>Mercury</term> with the white and the yolks of our Egg, let him know that he has come to the secret which the *Philosophers* call <term>Sulphur</term>. And Arnoldus <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist</note>:
> Although God has granted to every one of the animals and vegetables the perfect natural Stone and perfect Medicine, which has the power to tincture all metals into Gold or Silver:

The male is called the **Sun** <term>Sol: the masculine, active principle associated with gold</term>, the female is called the **Moon** <term>Luna: the feminine, passive principle associated with silver</term>. Therefore, Basen says in the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum," an influential early alchemical text</note>:

Likewise Arnoldus <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>:

> The **Physical Stone** <note>Latin: "Lapis Physicus"</note> is partly fixed and stable, and partly not fixed, but volatile <note>original: "flüchtig"; prone to evaporation or change when heated</note>. Otherwise, it could not have the nature of **Mercury** <note>Latin: "Mercurii"</note> and of a metal, between which it is the middle point. For the unstable nature is added to the stable nature, and after they are joined, they are embodied with one another, and one is made stable by the other.

Likewise, Morienus <note>A legendary hermit-philosopher said to have taught the secrets of alchemy to the King of Egypt</note> says of its volatile nature:

> Whatever you prepare for the work or **Mastery** <note>Latin: "Magisterio"; the completed alchemical process</note>, if you do not find the truth at its beginning, it is useless. For what good can be separated from it if the thing itself does not spring forth nor mix itself with itself in the world—namely, so that one single body may come from it?

> One should therefore praise God, who created something precious out of a lowly thing, so that it has a great fellowship with minerals in Nature. Therefore, it is the only thing that surpasses the Fire, and by it is not...

For with these, the various properties and the two colors of the single thing that the Stone <note>original: "Lapis"</note> has—namely Red and White—are indicated.

Among all these names, however, the names of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"</note> and **Moon** <note>original: "Lunae"</note> can be properly attributed to the Stone; but even more appropriately the names of **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphuris"</note> and **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>, and therefore also of **Arsenic** <note>original: "Arsenici"</note>, and most appropriately of all others, the name of **Mercury**.

And below he says:
> In all bodies of Alchemy, each planet makes its image in its place, until the completion of the Work.

Therefore, the **Sun** and **Moon** hold the beginning and the end. And just as in the beginning the Sun is hidden in the Moon, so in the end it is drawn out from the Moon and becomes manifest. But the Stone <note>original: "Lapis"</note> is more properly called Sulfur and Mercury, for it has their virtue and nature. Therefore Master Bonus says:
> Just as no child is born from the menstrual fluid <note>original: "menstruo"</note> without the man’s seed, nor can a bird be made from the four winds—for the power of the soul is not in them, but only in the man’s seed—likewise, no Gold or Silver can come from Mercury, nor any Elixir, without the action of Sulfur. For the generative power <note>original: "virtus generativa"</note> is not in it, except through Sulfur.

Also, just as nothing living can be born solely from the sperm or seed of the man without the menstrual fluid and matter of the woman—for the entire material of birth and nourishment comes from nowhere else but the woman—so also no Gold or Elixir can be made from Sulfur alone without Mercury. Therefore these two principles <note>original: "Principia"</note> must be mixed by nature and come together at once for the birth of the Elixir, just as they do for the generation of metals.

Therefore, the Sulfur cooks the Mercury with its action and gives it a metallic tincture <note>original: "tinctur"</note>, first a white one, then a red one. But Mercury, if it remains in its own nature—however pure and white it may be—does not tincture or color anything with its warmth and dryness. And this Stone has these properties, because of which the matter of the Stone is called "Arsenic" by Master Bonus under a figure <note>as a symbolic representation</note>, and not without reason. Of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij"</note>. For Arsenic has the natures, properties, and substance of Mercury mixed within itself, and it takes its place; it is the **Principle** <note>original: "Principium"</note> of Nature through this mixture, because it possesses its power and virtues. Therefore **Geber** <note>An influential 8th-century Arabic alchemist, known as the "Father of Chemistry"</note> says: There are three **Principles of Nature**, namely **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, **Sulfur**, and something equal to Sulfur, which is also Arsenic. *Likewise*: **Natural principles** <note>original: "Principia naturalia"</note> in the Work of Nature are a foul-smelling **spirit** and a living water, which we also allow to be called "dry water." For Mercury, when it is coagulated into an Arsenic, is a dry water. Thus **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemical author</note> calls the Stone "Arsenic" so that one may understand that Heat and Moisture are united within it, which are not the common Mercury or common Sulfur. Rather, it is a thing that possesses their virtues and properties. And this is done so that one may also understand that in the **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</term> of our Stone, one proceeds first to the Whiteness <note>The Albedo stage of the Great Work</note>, in whose belly the true and perfect Redness <note>The Rubedo, or final stage</note> lies hidden.

Therefore **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: You should know that Sulfur and the medicine—that is, **Orpiment** <note>original: "Auripigment"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>—are combustible, and are soon consumed by burning. How then can you expect or hope for anything from a thing that is easily and quickly consumed by fire and turned into a coal? Which words Master Bonus interprets, saying: that when one considers Arsenic and sees how it is created by Nature, it is entirely combustible, for the combustible Sulfur can never be separated from the other parts; rather, they vanish together. Likewise, in the "Lesser Work," when one **fixes** <term>Fixation: making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire</term> it in such a manner, it does not "enter" <note>meaning it does not penetrate or transform the metal</note>. But when one preserves its hidden nature, which is of the nature of Gold, then it is not combustible; for its hidden parts are separated from the **sulfurous** ones by the sharpest intellect. Therefore it appears that Morienus spoke figuratively of this, as he and all other **Philosophers** <note>Alchemists</note> are accustomed to do.

This Stone is also primarily called **Mercury** by the Philosophers because, according to its entire nature, it has the properties of Mercury and retains them in the beginning, middle, and end. In the beginning, indeed, because the Work starts from a volatile nature that has the same whiteness as Mercury. In the middle, however, because the entire Matter is brought to the most perfect Whiteness with a crystalline luster. In the end, although the Redness is drawn out from its hidden interior, the entire Matter is nonetheless **mercurial**. For the more perfect the **metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note> are, the more they have of Mercury and the less of Sulfur. For this reason alone, Gold is entirely deprived of Sulfur after its cooking is completed; and therefore it is...

## SECOND PART, CHAPTER 10.

It is also more indestructible and constant than all other **metals** <note>original: "Metall"</note>. And although **sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur"</note> begins to coagulate the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> and to tint it with many kinds of colors at the beginning: <margin>Note Well</margin> nevertheless, after long cooking, the **quicksilver** has the power within itself to coagulate and tint without another **sulfur**, or with very little **sulfur**.

For both Tinctures—the White and the Red—come from the two spirits: yet the white is specifically from **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, while the red is specifically from **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphure"</note>. Therefore, because **Mercury** has taken the virtue and substance of the **Elixir** <note>The "philosophers' stone" in its liquid or medicinal form</note> from the **Sulfur** during coagulation and cooking, it will also take from it the power to color and change every **Body** <note>original: "Corpus"; refers to a base metal</note> into a perfect **metal**. It will first change them into a White metal in the first cooking, and thereafter into a Red metal in the final cooking. Thus, the first Tincture is from **Mercury**, which it takes unto itself from the cooking **Sulfur**. The sign of this is that every **metal**, when it is purified, shows the nature of **coagulated Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij coagulati"</note> more than that of a **Sulfur** on the outside, because of its external abundance.

The second Tincture is also from **Mercury**, for the final form is drawn out from its material, and in this way the **Stone** <note>original: "Lapis"</note> is called **quicksilver**. And this **quicksilver** is drawn out from the **Bodies** and born from **quicksilver**, and it comes from a "male" <note>The masculine principle in alchemy, often associated with heat and sulfur</note> and is quickly coagulated by its body—that is, by the **Sulfur of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Sulphure Philosophorum"</note>, which is never separated from it.

And although **Mercury** draws its **Body** with it into flight <note>Meaning it vaporizes or sublimes</note>, that same **Body** quickly kills it <note>In alchemy, to "kill" Mercury means to "fix" it so it no longer vaporizes when heated</note> and keeps it with itself in the fire. Therefore **Rasis** <note>Rhazes, a 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist</note> says in the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "lumine luminum"</note>: The volatile and spiritual **Mercury** is the beginning of the whole Work and strengthens the root. Therefore **Sol** <note>The Sun, representing Gold</note> (as is said in that same place) takes on a female form at this point, because the nature of the Whiteness requires it so. But because the Redness eventually prevails, it is attributed to **Sol**. For even if it is truly and entirely Red, it nevertheless hurries first to the Whiteness because of the nature of **Mercury**, in which the root of the Redness is hidden, just as **red lead** <note>original: "minium"</note> is hidden in **white lead** <note>original: "Cerussa"</note>. Therefore **Pythagoras** <note>The Greek philosopher, often cited in alchemical texts as a legendary authority</note> says: **Sol** appears White to the eye, but is Red in experience. For this reason, **Rasis** calls this white gold a **neutral body** <note>original: "Corpus neutrum"</note>. And when this **Mercury** springs forth, **Sol** and **Luna** <note>The Sun and Moon, representing Gold and Silver</note> come out from its belly along with it. But when **Sol** rises at the same time, it holds and fixes the **Mercury** and hides it in its belly. Therefore, if **Sol** did not rise at the same time as the **Mercury** in its flight, it would not be united with it and would not fix it. For through this—because they rise together—the one takes the virtue over the other.

And therefore the **Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus"; the volatile or vaporous principle</note> then overcomes the **Body** <note>original: "Corpus"; the solid or fixed principle</note>, and the **Body** the **Spirit**, and they are transformed into one nature. From this, Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist known for his work *The Precious New Pearl*</note> concludes in chapter 5 that the origin of this same root and the foundation has been called **sublimated Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius sublimatus"</note>, and of this **Mercury** Rasis <note>The influential Persian physician and alchemist Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi</note> says: It dries, makes moist, makes cold, and warms it, and performs contrary effects according to its preparation. And Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, often considered the father of early chemistry/alchemy</note>: if you have not established a mitigation, then you will lose the whole **Work** <note>The "Great Work" or process of creating the Philosophers' Stone</note>. For the **Mercury** rising up in the **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and سپس solidifying it again for purification</note> together with its **Body** cannot be separated from it, regarding the substance and the place: Rather, they must necessarily either fly away together or remain together. <margin>Note Well</margin> But if the **Body** has obtained the power and dominion over the **Spirit**, it transforms it into its nature, and thus they remain henceforth in unity. But if the **Spirit** receives the power and dominion over the **Body**, then they both fly away and the Work comes to nothing. And this speculation is beautiful. For everything that is to be born and destroyed has its contrary and opposition within itself **in potential** <note>original: "poteſtate"; a philosophical term meaning a capacity that is not yet realized</note>, which can be brought **into action** <note>original: "in actum"; realized or manifest</note> without the presence and mixing of its external contrary. And in this way, that which was **fixed** <note>solid and heat-resistant</note> in potential, being reduced to an **unfixed** <note>volatile or vaporous</note> state in action, remains ours. Therefore Geber says: when the amount of the volatile exceeds the amount of the fixed, it flies away with it; but if the sum of the fixed exceeds the sum of the unfixed, they both become stable together. It is evident, however, that when the fixed exceeds the volatile, it makes the Work perfect; but if the volatile exceeds the fixed, it ruins the Work and brings it to nothing. Therefore it is said in the **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: Wage a war between the **ore** and **Mercury**, etc. To wage a war means as much as to destroy it, namely at the time when they wish to become united again after the war, and that is of the **Sun** <note>original: "Solis"; representing Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>original: "Lunae"; representing Silver</note>, of **Sulfur** and **Mercury**. In which one must so often make the volatile **fixed**, and vice versa, until they both become stable together and flow with transformation into a true **Gold** and **Silver**. And this **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> is increased with the gold, and vice versa, according to the philosophers. And because a single substance is the subject of both the fixed and the volatile, it is possible for the fixed to rise with the volatile, and conversely, for the volatile to be made stable with the fixed. And all of this happens in one vessel without manual grinding. From this it is clear that the **Stone** is properly called **Mercury**, even if it is also called the **Gold of the Philosophers** <note>original: "aurum Philoſophorum"</note> drawn from Mercury, and by many other countless names besides.

# C H A P T E R   X I I.
## Of the Regimen of the Stone in General.

Now that we have spoken of the **Material** <note>original: "Materi"</note> of the Stone, we will subsequently speak of its **Regimen** <note>original: "Regiment"; the specific management of heat and timing in the process</note>. For many know the Stone, but they do not know its Regimen. From this, it is to be known that very many who work in this Art—indeed, almost countless numbers—err in the knowledge of the **Material** <note>original: "Materiæ"</note>: and even more are deceived in its preparation. Therefore, very few come to the perfection of the Stone, and among thousands, hardly one. Thus it is said in the **universal way**: 
> Hardly anyone will bring this most excellent work to a good end without hindrance. 

And an artist must bring this work to its completion through much labor and many errors. And in the **Book of Saturn**: 
> Many have the **Stone** <note>original: "Lapidem"</note> and know it, but they do not know its **virtue** <note>original: "Tugent"; its inner power</note>: And even if they knew its virtue, it would still help them nothing if they did not also know its **operation** and effect. 

But one cannot know its effect except through the inspiration of God, or through the teaching and instruction of a Master. **Rhodianus** also says: 
> In this work of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimiæ"</note> many err, and few come to its perfection. 

The cause of this, however, **Hamis** points out in the **Assembly** <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous medieval alchemical text</note>: 
> The subtle airy moisture, with a watery one: and a watery one with an earthly dry one, are so united and composed that they can hardly

...or nevermore, except only by the most subtle understanding of the Artist <note>the alchemist or practitioner</note>, can they be separated from one another. Therefore, he is blessed who has received such an understanding in this world. For without this separation or setting apart, all laborers have toiled in vain. And because there is such great difficulty and hardship in this same separation and division, almost no one, or hardly one among all the Philosophers of the world, can arrive at the fruit of it. Therefore, no one should boast that he knows the Stone unless he knows how to separate the aforementioned humors <note>original: "humores"; refers to the liquid or volatile components within the matter</note> and moistures within the Stone. 

But whoever can perform this separation, and naturally combine the purer parts—namely the airy, spiritual, and most subtle ones—and make a medicine from them, he shall be a seeker of this precious perfection. And for this reason, <term>Morienus</term> <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> cautions the laborers when he says: "This is the root of this thing; that whoever desires to learn it must first receive his instruction from a teacher, so that afterwards the teacher may often perform and handle it before the student."

For there are many hindrances in this Art, and there is a great difference between a wise man and an unwise one, and between a blind man and one who sees. And he who has rightly recognized the disposition through trial <note>original: "probieren"; practical laboratory experimentation</note> is unequal to him who still hangs upon the investigation of books. From this, it is understood that every operation, whatever it may be, is necessary in our Mastership. For <term>Rosarius</term> <note>referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous alchemical treatise</note> says: Although our Stone already naturally contains its tincture <note>original: "tinctur"; the transformative power to change metals</note> within itself, because it is created perfectly in the body of <term>Magnesiæ</term> <note>alchemical Magnesia, a symbolic term for the "root" or crude matter of the Stone</note>, that is, the Earth; yet it does not have the motion <note>original: "Motum"; the active power to change</note> or movement by itself to become a perfect <term>Elixir</term> <note>the universal medicine or perfected Stone</note> unless it is moved through Art and operation. 

Therefore a Philosopher has said: "Son, extract from the stone its shadow." This is also said by <term>Mundus</term>, <term>Theophilus</term>, and <term>Hermes</term>. Therefore, such an operation is necessary for us, just as you see in a child who, as far as its creation is concerned, is born complete, but is yet imperfect regarding its activity unless it is first nourished. For this reason, many kinds of arts have been invented by the Philosophers, as a Philosopher says, so that through Art that which was left by Nature might be fulfilled. He is foolish who imagines false things for himself, or who says something true that is of no use.

The end of this operation, however, as <term>Geber</term> <note>the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century alchemist</note> says, is so that in our Stone the tincture might be improved more than it is in its own nature. <term>Bonellus</term> says: Nothing is made from the elements without a regimen <note>original: "regiment"; the strict governance of heat and timing in the furnace</note>, prepared with the highest diligence.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## What sort of regimen, in particular, is required in this Art.

What specific regimen <note>original: "Regiment"; here meaning the controlled management, sequence of operations, or "rule" of the alchemical process</note> is necessary for this Art must be investigated in the following. Some, however, have believed that the governance of the Stone <note>original: "Regiment Lapidis"</note> is a work of Nature alone, so that the artist does nothing more than enclose it in a vessel and hang it in the air in the shade where there is no wind, or bury it in the earth, paying attention to the appropriate season of the year, months, days, and hours, and the proper course of the planets and stars—so that Nature performs everything else until completion. Thus, the governance of the Stone would be nothing other than an arrangement in the proper place and time. This view seems to arise from observing how metals themselves, as well as stones and other minerals and growing things, are brought to their fulfillment within the belly of the Earth solely through heat and the power caused by the celestial bodies. 

And the <term>Rosarius</term> <note>Refers to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, or "Rosary of the Philosophers," a foundational 16th-century alchemical text</note> says: "Let it suffice you when you have rightly provided for the matter externally; for it can work sufficiently within itself toward perfection. For it possesses its own inherent movement, following a single path and a better and more certain order than could be devised by any man in the creation of any generated thing." Therefore, there must be such a preparation in the <term>Magistery of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Magisterio Philosophorũ"; the masterwork or the actual process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. For if Nature is not hindered through the center <note>original: "Centrum"; the internal core or vital point of the matter</note>, she cannot exceed her certain movement before she has the time to become pregnant, to give birth, to nourish, and to work.

From this, the argument is drawn—as the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists</note> say—that the cooking of the Stone must occur in the heat of the sun. Likewise, they distinguish the year into four seasons, and they say the Stone is to be governed according to their changes. For Zeno says in the <term>Turba</term> <note>Refers to the *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the earliest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>: "The year is divided into four parts: the first is Winter, cold and moist; the second is Spring, warm and moist; the third is Summer, warm and dry; the fourth is Autumn, cold and dry. In this manner, one must govern the two natures." Many other things also...

They have written of this: whoever reads the books of the philosophers and diligently examines them will find that the regimen of the Stone <note>original: "Regiment des Lapidis"; the controlled management or "rule" of the alchemical process</note>, made through art, cannot be made perfect without the warmth of fire. For all philosophers state that the <term>Magistery</term> <note>The "Great Work" or the mastery of the alchemical process</note> is performed with fire. Therefore, Morienus says: "Make the furnace of the philosophers in which you ignite the <term>physical fire</term>." <note>original: "ignem Physicum"; a specialized term for the heat used to drive alchemical transformations</note> And the same author says: "the great power of this work is preserved in the fire." For with fire the minerals are made ready, and the souls are better retained in their bodies, and with it the souls are joined together with the body; and fire is the true and perfect testing of this thing. From this, it is not to be understood that natural heat alone is enough; rather, one must also use elemental fire, as is evident from his other words that are set down hereafter.

Likewise, it is said in the *Book of Saturn*: the entire regimen of our work consists in the fire, in the vessel, and in the sealing; and truly, without these, our Magistery cannot be completed.

Likewise, Rhodianus says: the work of Mercury—which is seed, blood, and flesh—is thus created in the belly of the <term>athanor</term> <note>original: "Athanors"; a furnace designed to maintain a steady, uniform heat over a long period</note>, just like a child in the mother's womb.

And Bonedus says: From the elements, nothing useful is made without composition and regimen, because the sperm is born from blood and heat <note>original: "Geylheit"; literally "lecherousness" or "vigor," referring here to the vital, generative heat of the body</note>. For if the moisture and warmth of the belly were not present, the seed would not remain, and the birth would not be accomplished. Then, once the birth is brought forth, one must nourish it with milk and gradually with gentle fire while it is still young. And thus you must also do in this operation, and you should know that without warmth, nothing at all is generated.

Likewise: It is certain that in the generation of metals there must be a steady warmth; for they would be well-protected in their mineral vessels, but they would not be preserved if the mountain were not thick and solid, so that the surrounding cold drove the warmth together into the innermost parts. <term>Therefore, by analogy</term> <note>original: "Ergò à simili"</note>: the cooking of the Stone must necessarily be done with steady warmth held in a suitable vessel, which could not happen in the open air: for then the cooking would be altered now by too much cold, now by too much moisture, and then by other variations. And therefore Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher famous for his writings on the natural sciences</note> says in <term>Book 3 of "On Minerals"</term>: The warmth of the fire performs that which the sun's warmth carries out in the mountains. For in both cases, the power received from the planets and stars is directed into the vessels and poured into the things themselves. Likewise, the fire must be greater in the generation of the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The final, perfected substance capable of transmuting metals or healing the body</note> than in the birth of the elements:

### SECOND PART, CHAPTER 13.

Otherwise, if the warmth were equal on both sides <note>meaning the internal heat of nature versus the external heat of the artist</note>, there would have to be an equal amount of time in both generations, and thus in a thousand years the Elixir would not be completed. Therefore, as Master Bonus says in chapter 5 <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist from Ferrara, author of "The New Pearl of Great Price"</note>, there is another regimen for this same thing with the fire, where warmth is present on both sides. Consequently, there is one timeframe for the generation of metals <note>in nature</note>, but another for the generation of the Elixir <note>in the laboratory</note>.

From this it follows that one must provide the Work with a different, stronger, and more steady warmth through Art than Nature provides. For in this way, Art can fulfill the length of the natural effect <note>meaning Art speeds up the process that takes Nature centuries</note>. Therefore, *Rosarius* <note>Likely the "Rosarium Philosophorum" or "Rosary of the Philosophers," a central alchemical text</note> says: Practice diligently in the regimens, and you will arrive at the virtue, which is accomplished neither by itself nor in a miraculous way, as you might think, but through Art and action, with the high understanding of the Artist. Therefore, the philosophers likewise assert that this Art is a **work of women** and a **play of children**. And they have said this because the work of women is cooking, and one cannot cook without fire. Therefore, this work also cannot be performed without fire. It is, therefore, completed by the Artist with the fire that is added from the outside. But from this it is not concluded that Nature does not work along with it. For Nature completes everything; the Artist only applies what is necessary, and among other things, the fire as the most essential. **And this is true.** <note>original: "et hoc verum"</note>

Since the material is partially <term>fixed</term> <note>meaning stable or non-volatile</note>, one must give it fire from the beginning and maintain it until the end, yet moderately, so that the material gradually becomes accustomed to enduring the fire, until it finally becomes entirely fixed, so that it no longer fears any fire at all. For this is the end of the Art: that a <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur often represents the active, combustible, and coloring principle</note> or Elixir be born entirely incombustible, just as the end of Nature is that gold be born which is steadfast in the fire. This, however, can be achieved more conveniently by nothing other than the fire. For thus, through the power of fire, it is gradually strengthened and leans **toward incorruptibility**. <note>original: "ad incorruptibilitatem"</note>

Therefore, the regimen of this Art is the warmth and the fire, and not only the natural warmth, or that of a stone, or of the celestial bodies. It is also not necessary that you take heed of the rising and course of the heavenly signs, or the aspect of the planets, or of the time of year, or of the days and hours—except for what concerns the quality of the root, which will be discussed below. For the birth of this stone of ours is entirely natural, just like other things that Nature brings forth, as are its virtues, although it is to be called Divine and Heavenly because of its excellence and superiority, and also spirit-

### CHAPTER XIV.
#### That a good root belongs to the Governance <note>original: "Regiment"; refers to the management or "regimen" of the alchemical process</note>.

But before all things, you must have the very best root of the Stone of the Philosophers <note>original: "Lapidis Philoſophorum"</note>, otherwise nothing will come of it. For Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: the larger root of this work is better in the investigation of the forms which are better for the Mastery <note>original: "Magiſterio"; the completion of the Great Work</note>. For every mineral <note>original: "Minera"</note> has many kinds. And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: Take our Stone from the highest good, and do not take it unless it is new with all its blood. Likewise in the *Universal Way* <note>original: "via univerſali"</note>: The new species are better than the old. Mundus in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: Beware that you take no other ore than that which is pure and clean.

Therefore, in order to choose a good root, one must consider three things. First, that it be drawn from the best bodies. For from a good tree grow good apples; and from the better trees flow also the better gums; and from the better hens are also born better eggs; and a good food makes fat and good flesh. In general, black hens are better than white ones. Among the temperaments <note>original: "complexionen"</note>, the sanguine and choleric are the better ones; among the ages, the best and stronger is youth.

Therefore *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> says: You shall not eat from the Son whose Mother has the menstrual flow <note>original: "menſtruum"; here implying a state of impurity or corruption</note>; but if you wish to eat, then eat of the fatter flesh, so you will have Gold. And in the *Book of Saturn* it is said: You shall not eat from the Son whose mother is a leper <note>original: "auſſetzig"; in alchemy, "leprosy" refers to the impurities or corrosion found in base metals</note>. For if we have a pure substance, we can also make a pure Body; and if the Man is a leper and the Woman is also a leper, then a leprous Body <meta>catchword: pus</meta>

...body <note>original: "pus," completing "Corpus"</note> may become therefrom. Therefore, if we wish to make a pure body, we must have a pure man, clean of all filth, and likewise a pure seed that is free of all impurity. And Raymond <note>Likely referring to the famous medieval alchemist Raymond Lull</note> says in *On the Terms*: Take the gum of India, if you can get it, which is a black gum and clear on the outside, but red in its hidden interior; or take it from Spain; and join the man and the woman together at once.

The second thing to be observed is that the woman must be impregnated by her male seed. For the generation <note>the process of creation or birth</note> of the Stone is almost identical to the birth of a human, for both seeds—of the man and of the woman—must come together. But all the virtue <note>original: "tugent"; the inherent power or essential quality</note> that gives birth to the soul comes from the man’s seed. Therefore, just as no bird comes from "wind-eggs" <note>unfertilized eggs, which folklore suggested were produced by the wind</note>, so the Stone <note>original: "Lapis"</note> does not come from the Egg of the Philosophers unless the woman is impregnated by her man. And this seed is a fiery virtue, penetrating and coloring, and a coagulant <note>original: "coagulum"</note> or thickener that coagulates and thickens the menstrual blood <note>original: "menstruum"; in alchemy, this refers to a primary solvent or "first matter" rather than literal blood</note>; and it is a soul or subtle spirit that brings life. And therefore a Philosopher says: just as a human cannot be born without the joining of man and woman, so it is also with the Medicine <note>Another name for the Philosopher's Stone or the curative elixir</note>. For the man is warm and dry, but the woman is cold and moist; but when they are both joined together, the heat is tempered by the cold, and the dryness by the moisture. For an animal cannot easily be born if the heat exceeds the cold, or vice versa, etc. But in the mixing of both, the extremes are brought to a middle disposition, namely to a tempered warmth. For the life of animals consists of moisture and heat, but in a tempered state, as Aristotle <note>the Greek philosopher whose theories on the four elements were foundational to alchemy</note> teaches.

So it is also in all things with our unique Stone, which is not only composed of a twofold nature, namely man and woman (as was said above), according to which they act and suffer upon one another, perfecting and completing themselves, as will appear in what follows; but it is also conceived and born from its first origin, from the seed of the woman and the menstrual blood. For this reason, it is even called an "animal," because it has life in potential <note>original: "potestate"</note> and is always fluid; and because it is a domestic animal, it has not unjustly been called a "human."

Hence it is said in the *Book of Saturn* <note>a classic alchemical text</note>: concerning the first and second creation of this Stone, it is said that when the man is united with the woman through a tempering by means of the seed, it is necessary that a birth occurs from the menstrual blood. ## THE NEW ROSARY

The thing from which the Stone <note>original: "Lapis"</note> is made is called *Rebis* <note>A Latin-derived term meaning "a double thing" or "two-fold matter"</note>; that is, a thing that is put together twice, and a thing that is composed of two. And he spoke truly. For it is composed at once and at one time in the Book of the Earth—which is the Mother—so that it may be born: and for the second time, it is put together in a glass vessel so that it may be made into an Elixir. The two things, however, from which it is composed, are the seed of the man and the menstrual blood <term>menstruo: in alchemy, this refers to a primary solvent or "first matter" thought to nourish the Stone, rather than literal blood</term> of the woman; that is, it is born from a Red and a White: also between two mountains, which are Father and Mother. Others, however, understand the two mountains to be Sulfur and Mercury, or the Sun <note>original: "Solem"</note> and the Moon <note>original: "Lunam"</note>, but these people are considering the properties of the Stone within itself: and therefore it contains within itself the qualities of a man and a woman.

The third thing that one should observe is that it be taken at the very best time. For then every thing is truly useful to man when it is in its own nature and at its most perfect. But our Stone, just as it is found everywhere, so too is it found at every time: but it does not possess the same virtue <note>original: "tugent"; meaning its inherent power or efficacy</note> at every time, just as it does not in every place. Every growing thing has its own time: every fruit and little herb is at its best when it is ripe. Thus our Stone is better in two respects: firstly, regarding the time, namely when it springs forth in the Spring, while other gums <term>Gummi: often used to describe the viscous, resin-like consistency of the alchemical substance</term> are ripened by the summer heat and flow out then. For our gum is best poured out in the time of Spring. Because it is most closely related to the nature of human blood, and draws near to the procreation of the animals—when the animals are incited to mate and the birds to brood—therefore our matter <note>original: "materia"</note> of the Stone should also be sought then. It is then most fit for the Work, so that our flying bird may be brought forth, whether it has feathers or is without feathers <note>The "flying bird" is a common alchemical metaphor for a volatile substance that rises as vapor during heating</note>.

Therefore, Raymond [Lull] says in *On Terms* <note>original: "Raymundus de terminis"</note>: Place our Stone in the physical vessel <note>original: "vas Physicum"; the alchemical flask designed to mimic natural processes</note> in the Spring, when the Sun is in the Ram <term>Wider: the zodiac sign of Aries, which begins the astrological year at the Spring Equinox</term>. For at this time (as Raymond of Marseilles <note>original: "Raymundus Massiliensis"</note> says) the warmth and moisture, as well as the blood and choler <term>Colera: one of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with fire and yellow bile</term>, are most increased. And therefore this element of the Stone is most abundant in the Spring, and in such a way Nature helps Art, and Time helps the Work, and the Plants <note>original: "Plantæ"</note> help the Mastery <note>original: "Magisterio"; the completion of the Great Work</note>.

Secondly, it is also better when it is still new. For new and young fruits are better than the old when they are ripe: for born from each thing that is plucked from its roots, it becomes...

## CHAPTER XV.
# That a Suitable Vessel Belongs to the Governance.

There is also something else necessary for the governance <term>Regiment: the controlled management of the alchemical process, especially the heat</term> and preparation of the Stone; namely, a suitable vessel. Therefore, after you have recognized the good roots <note>The foundational materials or primary principles of the work</note>—which is the first step—you must also recognize a suitable vessel—which is the second—in which the Stone is born as if in its own proper place. For every thing is born in its suitable place. Therefore, this most wonderful vessel is highly necessary for the Stone. Hence Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist often cited as a teacher to the King Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: "If the wise had not discovered their dispositions <note>original: "dispositiones"; the specific arrangement or setup of the work</note> from the size and quality of the vessel in which the Stone is made, they could never have attained the perfection of the Mastery <note>original: "Magisterij"; the completed alchemical work</note>."

For I have indicated above that this mastery has no great difference from the birth of a human being. For the birth of a human is completed in no other way than in the mother's womb. For young animals are tempered, nourished, and perfected out of the warm moisture from the mixture of seeds, as Morienus says: just as the metals are born in the womb of the earth that cooks them. Birth occurs in the womb, just as a young chick <note>original: "Hünlein"</note> is born in the shell. 

One must, however, deduce and determine the properties and conditions of the vessel from the nature of the Stone itself. For the Stone cannot be made perfect unless its entire virtue is kept within the vessel. Therefore, this vessel in which the Mastery is performed must, first of all, be very strong so that it may endure the fire. Thus it is said in the *Lily* <note>original: "Lilio"; likely referring to the *Lilium Philosophorum* or "Lily of the Philosophers," a popular alchemical text</note>: "This stony and round vessel must not fear the fire, nor must it be gapped or porous, but very thick and solid." 

Therefore, it is said in the *Book of Saturn* <note>original: "libro Saturni"</note>: "Many have made earthen vessels, or even of iron, and were finally deceived, for the spirits <term>Spiritus: the volatile vapors or "souls" of the chemicals</term> fly out through the tiny pores, and therefore they did not arrive at the perfection of the Mastery."

# NEW ROSARY

Thirdly, the vessel should be made of glass and of a single material. Because glass is created in the fire, it can endure the fire better than all other materials. Glass is also solid and has no tiny pores <note>original: "schweiß-löchlein," literally "sweat-holes"</note>; therefore, the spirits cannot leak out <note>original: "herauß riechen," literally "smell out"</note>, as is stated in the same book. But if it were made of any other material, whatever it might be, it would be of no use.

Fourthly, it must be good and thick. For this reason, the *Lilium* <note>Referring to the alchemical text *Lilium Intelligentiae*</note> says: among these stone vessels that the glassmakers use, few endure without being corroded or broken during the Work. Therefore, Morienus says: "place them mixed into a thick vessel." *In the universal path* <note>original: "In via univers."</note>: Each part should be placed separately in a double-glass urinal <term>Urinal: a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, common in medieval laboratories</term>.

Fifthly, it must have a round belly and a long, narrow neck. Therefore Pandulphus and Horfoleus say: It shall be round, or like the celestial Moon. And *in the universal path*: the vessels should be glass, having a round belly and a neck half a foot long, and narrow at the top, yet wide enough that you may put your thumb into it; and they should be shaped like a phial <note>original: "viol"</note>, and be thick and strong; otherwise, they cannot hold that same water, but would break because of its great strength.

Sixthly, one vessel is enough. Therefore the *Lilium* says: One should know that the Philosophers assign only one vessel to our Work. For whenever they speak of the operation, they always name only one vessel *in the singular*. Thus Bonellus says: "Lay it in its vessel." Xistus also says: "put it in its vessel with a narrow neck." And *in the Book of Saturn*: everything is completed in one vessel and not in many. And Geber: and this all happens in one furnace and in one vessel. This is, therefore, the wonderful vessel that is called by so many names. For first, it is commonly called the "Vessel of the Philosophers," invented by the Philosophers alone as that which is most suitable for the Work. It is also called the "Egg of the Philosophers," because it is shaped like an egg. It is also called a *Sublimatorium* <term>Sublimatorium: a vessel used for sublimation, where a substance is heated to a vapor and then solidifies again</term>, because the Stone <note>original: "Lapis"</note> is sublimated within it. It is also called a "Sieve." For within it, the Stone falls down drop by drop, just like water through a sieve. Therefore Mireris says: "One must sift it through its sieve." It is also called a "Sphere," for it is shaped exactly like a sphere; and because within it the Stone is rolled and driven upward and downward, as if moving *circularly in its orbit*. Therefore Mireris says: "Seek the sphere and you shall find" <note>original: "Spera sperata & invenies"</note>. And Ascanus: "One must sift the gold of the sphere <note>original: "aurum Sphæræ"</note> seven times through a sieve." It is also called a "Grave." For in it...

### CHAPTER XVI.

->That the way of placing the Stone into its vessel<-
->is varied; and it is necessary to know<-
->which way is suitable or<-
->unsuitable.<-

There are many who know the Stone <note>original: "Lapidem"</note>, yet do not put it correctly into its vessel, and therein they do not achieve what they seek. And in this, there is a two-fold error. The first is indeed of those who separate the Man from the Woman, and join the Men with the Men separately, and the Women with the Women also separately together. And these are deceived by the words of the Philosophers, about which Alphidius <note>original: "Alphytris," likely referring to the alchemist Alphidius</note> Aristeus has composed, when he went into the depths of the sea; there he found the King and his people, who were not born, who absurdly joined the Men to the Men, and the Women to the Women, and laid the King’s son with his sister, whereby the King’s son died immediately.

The other error is of those who mix the whole Stone with "frost" <note>original: "reifen," which can mean frost or a specific white sublimate</note> and thus place it mixed into the vessel. And these are likewise deceived by the sayings of the Philosophers. For Morienus says: "Take the white and red smoke <term>smoke: refers to the volatile vapors or 'spirits' of the substance</term>, and pour them both out, and place them mixed in the vessel that is thick." And Aristeus: "Take the body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> that I have shown you and make thin tablets from it." But the Philosophers speak quite rightly, if one pays proper attention to their words. For one must note four things in this placement: the first is indeed that the Man and the Woman, Sun and Moon, Sulphur and Mercury, the Red and White—which is all one thing—should be put into the vessel at the same time; and one shall nevermore be separated from the other. For it is written: what God has joined together, man shall not separate. And above it is said, that the Man

But Sun <note>original: "Sol," representing gold or the male principle</note> and Moon <note>original: "Luna," representing silver or the female principle</note> are joined together in the birth of the Elixir in Art <note>Art: the practice of alchemy</note>, just as they are in Nature. Therefore *Mireris* says: Take the Stone and mix the White into the Red, and make it like a dough within dough. And the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Mundus in Turba," likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says: Beware that you do not take the ore unless it be pure and clean: lay these two neatly and whitely into the vessel, and pray to God that you may see this Stone mixed in the Work. And thus one understands the word of the *Hermetics*: Take the Stone of Gold <note>original: "Lapidem auri"</note> and mix it with the moisture, that is, with the permanent water. And again: if there were no ferment <term>ferment: a substance, often compared to yeast, that transforms and "leavens" the base matter into gold</term>, then the water would not be coagulated; for this reason it is called the "coagulating curd" <note>original: "coagulum coagulans"</note> by *Mary the Prophetess* <note>Maria Prophetissa, a famous early female alchemist often credited with inventing the bain-marie</note>. And *Socrates*: The secret of the Work is made from Man and Woman. For the Woman rejoices in the nature and virtue of the Man. And *Raymond [Lully]* on boundaries: join the Man to the Woman at the same time. And *on the universal way*: The two seeds must rest in this Work until they are mixed. And under this figure *Hermes* says: My son and my rays <note>original: "streimen"</note> are inside me. And this is the dream of *Rafis* <note>Rhazes, a Persian polymath and alchemist</note> to *Euthesia*, of a man who is to be killed, who had a white body like salt and a golden head, and was divided all around. And this is the vision of *Senior* <note>Senior Zadith, a 10th-century alchemist</note> who, in the prison of Joseph, saw the spheres of the Sun and the Moon. And *Aretus* says: Take the Man and the Woman purified, and pour them together in equal weight, so that through the Woman the Man is taken, that nothing more of the Man may be seen. Thereafter make very subtle thin sheets from it, then cut them and lay them in a glass house. *Rafis in the Assembly* also says: You sons of doctrine <note>original: "filij doctrinæ"</note>, lead the Red Man with his wife into the bath after the joining. And again: One should make a grave and bury the Woman with the dead Man in horse manure <note>Horse manure was used in alchemy as a source of gentle, steady heat for digestion or fermentation</note>; that is, one should cook them in moist warmth until they join together of their own free will.

They are therefore not mixed by force, but voluntarily; not through rubbing, but through warmth; not outside of the vessel, for they are already mixed and joined together by Nature.

It consists [of a matter] to which we must add nothing external, nor take anything away from it, except that in its preparation we remove the superfluity. And Diomedes in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: Use the venerable nature, for nature is not improved except within its own nature, to which you shall add nothing external, neither dust nor any other thing.

Thirdly, before one puts the Stone into the vessel, one must first remove its superfluity. And this is its cleaning, which is accomplished through infusion and pouring. Nothing superfluous and nothing lacking is found in our Stone. Therefore, the infusion is its purification, because the <term>Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapis"</note> is entirely pure in its nature. For this reason, in the <term>universal way</term> <note>original: "via universali"</note> no mention is made of the cleaning of our white and red earths, because they are found for sale sufficiently cleaned and purified. In its own house a flying bird is born; and in a foreign one a tinging <note>The power of a substance to transform and "color" base metals into gold or silver</note> stone: both birds give thanks upon the King's table and heads; for both birds—the one with wings and also the one without wings—have given this visible art, and they cannot leave the company of men. Its Father awakens the lazy to work; the Mother feeds those who have become weary through labor, refreshes their tender souls, and adorns them. Therefore, tear apart the house, break down the walls, draw out the very purest juice with the blood, and cook it so that you may eat it. Regarding this, Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a medieval physician and alchemist</note> says in the *Book of Secrets* <note>original: "lib. Secretorum"</note>: Clean the stone, rub the door, break the shell <note>original: "caniculam," literally "little dog," but here used metaphorically for a hard outer casing or husk</note>, take from it the tender flesh, and you shall have the very best thing. Therefore, in a single thing all members lie hidden, and all metals shine within it. These are two artists, two vessels, two times, two fruits, two ends, and one holy thing.

### PART TWO CHAPTER XVII.

spoiled. For as soon as the Stone is placed in the vessel, it begins, because of the narrowness of its imprisonment, to sweat, and the most subtle parts begin to rise; and the longer it is cooked, the more the spirits <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> are increased, refined, and strengthened. Therefore, one must immediately at the beginning close the glass and secure it with a strong seal <note>original: "sigill"</note>, so that the bloom <note>original: "blust," referring to the volatile essence or vapors</note> does not fly away and the entire Mastery <note>original: "Magisterium"</note> be lost. What use would it be to have a very strong vessel if it were not closed in the strongest and best way? But it is also not enough that it is merely strong; rather, it must also be a completely thick and firm closure, which is achieved when it has no "sweat-holes" <note>tiny pores or leaks in the seal</note>.

Therefore, all **Philosophers** advise that the vessel be sealed very strongly. Regarding this, **Mundus** says: Seal the mouth of the vessel firmly.
**Theophilus**: Seal the mouth of the vessel firmly, so that the flowers <note>original: "flores," the sublimated vapors that rise like blossoms</note> do not evaporate away.
**Artephius**: Put it into a glass house and seal it with lute <note>original: "Leimen," a specialized alchemical paste used to make joints airtight</note> in the very best way, so that the air does not go in and the enclosed moisture does not smell its way out.
And in the ***Book of Saturn*** <note>original: "lib. Saturni"</note> it is said: Put our Stone with its entire substance into our vessel, and seal it very well, so that nothing of it evaporates.
And **Morienus**: Seal the mouth of the vessel with resin, so that the winds do not flee from it. For in the long run, the winds are increased and become quite hot, so that it is to be feared that either the vessel will break or the seal will open.
Regarding these winds, **Haly** said figuratively: You should know that the roots of their minerals are in the air, and their heights in the earth; and when they are pulled out of their places, a terrible sound is heard, and there will be great fear: go quickly, for they soon vanish.
And therefore it is said in the ***Book of Saturn***: You should know that the entire Mastery consists in the fire and in the vessel; for if the mouth of the vessel is not well closed, the spirits <note>original: "Spiritus"</note>, which are very subtle, will flee away, and the entire Mastery will come to nothing.

Therefore, two kinds of danger are to be feared if the vessel is not well closed: first, that the effort and labor will be lost, as has been said. Secondly, that it may kill or harm the artist. For from the beginning, our Stone is like a deadly poison; in the middle, it is like a violent and subtle spirit that penetrates everything; in the end, it is like a medicine that heals perfectly.
Therefore **Artephius** says: Two things are to be avoided in the Mastery of the Stone: first, that it be not ignited by the fire; secondly, that it does not evaporate, for it harms the laborer <note>original: "Laboranten"</note> and brings him many sicknesses. Therefore it is necessary that one seals the vessel at its strongest, and with a single seal, not with many.

# SECOND PART CHAPTER XVIII.

...it is necessary to know the nature of his furnace, as well as the ascent of the fire, namely in which part of the furnace or at which place the fire should be ignited. And concerning this, three things are to be noted. First, a correct disposition of the furnace and a suitable proportion of the fire, so that it is neither too large nor too small, nor too high nor too suppressed; and that the walls are neither too thick nor too thin, but rather made such that it receives, retains, and gives off a sufficient and steady warmth.

For a large furnace or a small one, as well as a thin or a thick one, are not heated with equal and steady warmth. Therefore, Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist often cited as a teacher of King Khalid</note> says: When you make the furnace of the philosophers as mentioned above, in which you ignite the philosophical fire, then its material shall or will be made either of dung or of oil-soaked leaves <note>original: *öl blettern*</note>, which is nothing other than an equal and steady fire. Secondly, one should see to it that the heat touches the vessel everywhere at the height of the material equally. For this reason, Mireris <note>An alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a name from the Arabic tradition</note> says: Bury the vessel in a fiery nature. After you have established the fiery nature below and all around it, you must cover the vessel that stands in the middle with two or three fingers' thickness of the fiery nature, until it takes on the color of honey or of red sulfur. And Raymond de Terminis <note>Likely referring to a work attributed to Raymond Lull</note> says: Place the vessel in the **Bath of the Philosophers** <term>balneum Philosophorum<gloss>A gentle heating method where the vessel is placed in a medium like sand, ash, or water to distribute heat evenly</gloss></term>, so that the seeds can surround the vessel all around. And in the *Book of Saturn* <note>original: *lib. Saturni*</note>: place the vessel in the furnace, put ashes beneath it and along the sides, and two parts of the vessel should be left uncovered from above, and the third part covered, and prepare the fire well in the furnace. PART TWO, CHAPTER 19.

## CHAPTER XIX.

### That in our process no other action
### is performed by hand, except
### only by the fire.

---

It has already been stated that fire is necessary in our **Mastery of the Stone** <note>original: *Magisterio Lapidis*; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. However, it has not yet been explained whether other actions belong to it, such as **calcination** <term>calcinatio; heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term>, **sublimation** <term>sublimatio; the process of a substance turning from solid to vapor and back to solid</term>, **distillation** <term>distillatio</term>, **separation of the elements** <note>original: *separatio elementorum*</note>, **incineration** <note>original: *incineratio*; burning to ashes</note>, and other such actions which are said to occur in the **governance of the Stone** <note>original: *regimine Lapidis*; the controlled stages of the alchemical work</note>. Furthermore, many repetitions, weights, and different times are often cited. But if someone examines the books of the Philosophers correctly, he will find that in this Mastery there is only one single action and **confection** <term>preparation or mixture</term>; all the other actions they speak of are handled and accomplished by the fire alone. For **Magister Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century physician and alchemist who wrote "The Precious New Pearl"</note> says in Chapter 2: They all agree that there is one single, determined time for the cooking to complete the white and red **Elixir** <note>the final transformative substance</note>, even though they sometimes change and interrupt the timing in their teachings so that they might lead the **sophists** <note>here meaning fraudulent alchemists or "puffers"</note> into error.

And **Hamis** <note>likely referring to an Arabic alchemical authority like Al-Hamis</note> says: the **philosophers** <note>alchemists</note> say many things which they do not actually do themselves. For there is one way and one thing; therefore, you do not need to rub with your hands, or boil, or pour in any way as do those beginners who command such things. For it is a single **tincture** <note>original: *tincturam*; a substance that can color or "stain" a base metal into gold or silver</note> which they have called a tincture. Our lead, when it stands in **putrefaction** <note>original: *putrefactione*; the stage of decay or the "blackness" (nigredo)</note>, is called bronze or ore; when the moisture of the risen **Living Silver** <note>original: *Argenti vivi*; Mercury</note> ends, they call it putrefaction. But after the departure of the blackness toward the **citrine** <term>lemon-yellow</term> red color, they call it gold. But when it is from the third tincture, it is called the **Flower of Gold** <note>original: *Flos auri*</note>; when it is from the fourth, it is called **ferment** <note>original: *fermentum*</note> or doughy. But when it is from the last, it is called a **Theriac** <note>original: *Tiriac*; historically a "universal" medicine or antidote, here representing the ultimate healing power of the Stone</note> or serpent's venom.

In the same place: the Sages have composed their books in figures and metaphors so that they might blind the unwise. I say to the wise, however, that there is one work, one way, one thing, one governance—which is the action of the changing of natures—namely, a miraculous mixing of the hot with the cold, and the moist with the dry. Therefore **Mixeris** <note>an alchemical authority cited in the Turba</note> and many others in the **Gathering of Philosophers** <note>original: *Turba*; referring to the "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> say: with one disposition, the whole...

### NEW ROSARY

All elements are weighed according to natural and true proportion. And therefore, if the artist does not know the determined time for the purification of these same elements, he necessarily cannot know their weight and composition, and consequently can know nothing at all. Therefore, it is said in *The Light of Lights* <note>original: *Lumine luminum*; a medieval alchemical treatise often attributed to Aristotle or Rhazes</note>: weight should never depart from your memory. But because of this opinion, the Work is made quite difficult. For as far as the work of "cooking" is concerned, it is called "women’s work" <term>Weiberwerck; a common alchemical phrase implying that once the materials are properly prepared, the process of heating them is as simple and routine as domestic chores</term>, because it is indeed extremely easy. But as for the moderation of the governance <term>Regiment; the systematic control of heat and the timing of chemical stages</term> and the degrees of the fire, then it is most difficult of all.

Hence **Morienus** <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who supposedly taught the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note>, when speaking of two operations, says: this composition does not happen by the hands—a difficulty about which many **Philosophers** <note>the "Philosophers" usually refers to the collective authority of ancient and medieval alchemical writers</note> have complained. Therefore, the philosophers have set down nothing of their matters except according to the aforementioned weights, and have hidden nothing else. Thus, if we now believe (as **Petrus Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, author of the 14th-century *Precious Pearl*</note> says, chapter 5) that all the operations described by **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century polymath and "father" of Islamic alchemy</note> always come together at once in one vessel, without any grinding by the hands. For the fire alone "grinds" the whole material to complete both **tinctures** <term>Tincturen; the transmuting agents or medicinal essences capable of changing the nature of a substance</term> at the same time.

In this "grinding," however, the artist must use his hands and eyes very often, as assistants and **servants of Nature**: but not because it is ground with the hands, but because one cannot attain the science unless one sees it, as is said in the *Commentary on the [Apostolic?] Wisdom* <note>original: *Commento stolicarum*; likely a reference to a commentary on philosophical or ecclesiastical texts</note>. And therefore Geber says: if an artist does not have his perfect limbs, he will not be able to bring this Work to completion by himself—namely if he is blind or otherwise lacks hands and feet. And the third instrument and tool, above the two aforementioned, is a high understanding: that through his intellect he may grasp the works hidden within Nature from the things he sees, and also perceive the Divine operation which is above Nature. For if natural aptitude does not come to his aid—regardless of what knowledge he has otherwise gained through his study—he will not be invited to such a precious banquet (as Geber says), and could not correct an error at that point, for which he would know no remedy to apply.

From this it clearly appears that our **Stone** <term>Lapis; the Philosopher's Stone</term> stands in need only of the governance of the fire; for it has within itself the whole and perfect natures, in which it has sufficiency; it dissolves itself, coagulates itself, makes itself white, and makes itself red, and can govern itself. Yet all things are completed by means of the fire. For the fire first draws out the water, and by means of the water and fire, everything is accomplished.

# C H A P T E R XX.
## That in the governance of the stone there are not many degrees of fire.

Some have believed that in the **governance** of the fire, many **degrees** <note>graduated levels of heat</note> are to be administered according to the difference of time, in order to bring forth various effects, colors, and natures; and they believe that the sayings of the **Philosophers** make it appear as if they required such a thing. Therefore, it makes it appear as if the fire should be increased a little after the whiteness appears. Likewise, another **Philosopher** in the *Assembly* says: One must burn the ore with the other part of the water, so that it becomes soft in the water at the same time. Phidius says: Whenever you have poured the water over the earth, strengthen the fire in the **calcination** <term>the reduction of a substance to powder or ash through heat to purify it</term>, until through the alternating of water and fire all impurity is removed. And **Lilium** <note>The Lily, a common title for alchemical treatises</note>, in citing the words of **Rosinus to Euthesia** <note>original: *Rosini ad Euthesiam*; an alchemical dialogue attributed to Zosimos of Panopolis</note>, says: There are four seasons of the year: Winter, Spring, Summer, and Autumn. > If the thing that improves it is not within that very substance, then that which you seek will not come from it. For it is truly within the substance to make it better, provided it is not driven away with too much fire or with too much haste; and therefore patience and delay are necessary.

Hence **Zinon** <note>Zeno</note> says: 
> If one who enters this Art knew its nature, he would certainly endure the long duration of the cooking until, by the grace of God, he achieved his purpose from it. 

And **Morienus** says: 
> The artist should know the lighting of the fire, the number of its days, and its weight and measure.

From this it is now clear that the fire should be constant until the end of the work. If, however, it is sometimes commanded that one should make a stronger or larger fire, this is not to be interpreted as a greater temperature, but rather as a longer duration of time.
