## C H A P T E R  XXI.
### That the Fire should always be gentle and constant.

Since, however, there are many **degrees** <term>gradus; the different intensities or stages of heat</term> of fire, one must now examine how great it should be—whether it should be strong or weak. To answer this: first, the fire should be mild and gentle. Hence **Lilium** <note>The *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous alchemical text</note> says: You should know that nothing is ever born without warmth, and that great heat destroys, while cold quickly drives away that which is combined. But through a tempered fire, the body becomes lovely and suitable. For through a mild fire, the destructive moisture is drawn out; for the **Philosophers** <term>the alchemists of antiquity</term> all testify that they have found no other fire that draws out the destructive moisture except a soft and mild one. 

By this, they wish to recommend duration and patience, and simultaneously rebuke haste, as is right. For if the **composite** <term>the mixed alchemical substance</term> or the combined thing is governed more than is proper, it is destroyed. And in the **Book of Saturn** <note>original: *lib. Saturni*</note> it is said: The entire operation lies in the governance of the fire. For whoever knows how to govern the fire reaches perfection. 

The one who governs his matter with mild fire can reach the secret, and thus the matter does not turn into glass, but remains always dissolvable. But with great and strong fire, it turns into glass, and becomes so hard that it cannot be dissolved except with great labor, which is of no use. For one must separate the subtle parts from the coarse, and the **fixed** <term>stable and non-volatile</term> from the **unfixen** <term>volatile or unstable</term>; this, however, happens only with mild fire. For if the fire is too strong, either the matter is burned, or the coarse parts rise up together with the subtle ones and kill them. 

And therefore all **Philosophers** desire a gentle fire. Hence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: Separate the earth from the fire, and the subtle from the coarse, being gentle with great understanding. And **Morienus** <note>a 7th-century legendary hermit and alchemist</note> says: What makes these bodies primarily suitable is the **oily nature** <term>original: *Oleaginari*</term>. For it makes them living and joins them together, and one **Body** <term>original: *Corpus*</term> is made from them all. For this reason, a very gentle fire should be made and applied...

<summary>This chapter stresses the absolute necessity of maintaining a gentle, tempered heat during the alchemical process. It warns that excessive fire leads to vitrification—turning the matter into useless glass—whereas a mild heat allows for the proper separation of subtle and coarse elements.</summary>

...be, so that its day lasts equally throughout. Because through the heat of the fire, which creeps quickly into the body with rapid burning, the **body** is consumed. ### SECOND PART CHAPTER XXI.

...is divided into parts / etc. Which does not happen / except through a gentle fire / which among the Philosophers is called the heat of the Sun / for it is gentle like the sun’s warmth. For a strong fire destroys and scatters the Work. But a mild fire leads to health / and gives birth to a single substance. And as **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and "father of chemistry" whose Latinized works were central to alchemical study</note> says: A gentle fire preserves the **natural and radical humidity** <note>original: *naturalem vnd radicalem humiditatem*; the essential, deep-seated moisture believed to be the life-force of the substance</note> / and allows for the **flow** <term>the state in which a substance becomes fluid and can penetrate or transmute other metals</term>.

This Governance / however / you can learn from two things / first that you turn yourself toward Nature / and then also toward the books. You should therefore first imagine Nature clearly. For Nature performs her cooking completely and steadily through the heat of the sun in the womb of the earth / until metals are generated from the **mineral spirits** <note>original: *spiritibus mineralibus*</note> of the vapors: So you should also govern your Art / and you will find it perfected. ### THE NEW ROSARY

And these have almost all been deceived: for we have now but one fire, and the same is with the **Philosophical wick** <term>Philosophical wick</term> <note>original: *Philosophischen docht*; a legendary incombustible wick used in "ever-burning lamps," often associated with mineral fibers that do not consume away.</note>. This wick, however, does not burn away, nor does it become less. It is instead made from prepared **talc** <note>original: *talch*; in this context, likely referring to asbestos or "Salamander’s wool," which resists fire.</note> with silk threads or with willow threads—that is, those made from the sponge-like fungus that grows on the willow trees. Therefore, the artist has nothing else to do but only to pour in the oil. With such a fire our **Work** is transformed and not otherwise. For I have already taught that a great fire is a cause of error, but a gentle fire is a cause of perfection. Therefore, the Philosophical fire should be from a wick of three threads, and the threads should not be coarse. 

From this conclude now that our Philosophical fire is the fire of the Sun, of the Bath, of the Manure, and of the Lamp. For it is all just one thing: that it always burns steadily. Except perhaps in the final **reddening** <note>original: *rotmachung*; the *Rubedo* stage, the final phase of the alchemical process where the Stone achieves its full power.</note>, when the **Sulfur** <note>In alchemy, Sulfur represents the active, combustible, and soul-like principle of a substance.</note> has been made entirely and utterly incombustible; then the fire is strengthened a little, yet as if imperceptibly. 

For in this way the airy **Spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*</note> is first drawn out with the water. Afterward, the **Soul** <note>original: *Anima*</note>, which is the Sulfur or dissolved **tincture**; which, when it has been given back to the **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note>, is made alive by the Body and becomes gradually accustomed to enduring the fire, until it finally fears it no longer. 

Therefore the **Stone** <note>original: *Lapis*</note> finally comes to such perfection that it flows in the fire like an oil; but in the air, which is a little cold, it becomes hard like pitch or wax. And yet it is never diminished in the fire, even if it stood in the fire for a thousand years. And because there is a fire within the fire, one should draw it to the fire until it no longer fears the fire, as **Calid** says in the **Turba** <note>Refers to Khalid ibn Yazid, a legendary Umayyad prince and alchemist, often quoted in the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>. 

And this is the **Oil of the Philosophers** <note>original: *Oleum Philosophorum*</note> made from the joining of the Body and the Soul, from which Body the Soul was previously drawn by the "subtle" part—which is the Water and an airy vapor—which is not joined back to the Body except by means of the Soul. And therefore the Soul, which was drawn out of the Body, must first be united with the Spirit, so that they both may afterward be joined to the Body, make the Body alive, and reveal the hidden nature. This oil, however, should be separated with warmth and moisture; otherwise one cannot have it, as a Philosopher writes to his son **Thomas** <note>Likely referring to pseudonymous works attributed to Thomas Aquinas.</note>. For with moisture the water is drawn out; with warmth the soul; and the water protects the Body from burning, but the Soul colors and

->tinctures it with a constant and permanent<-
->color.<-

This process results in the "Oil of the Philosophers," a substance that flows like oil in heat but hardens in air and remains entirely unconsumed by fire.</summary>

## CHAPTER XXII.
->**That the **Stone** <term>Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapis*</note> is completed at a determined**<-
->**time.**<-

**F**urthermore, we wish to speak of the time—in how long a time the **Stone** <term>Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapis*</note> may be brought to completion—concerning which the **Philosophers** <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original: *Philosophi*; referring to the ancient and medieval alchemists.</note> have written many different things. For some indicate a short time, and others a long one, as can be seen in ***The Lily*** <term>The Lily</term> <note>original: *Lilio*; likely referring to the *Lilium Artis* or *Lilium Alchimiae*, a famous alchemical treatise attributed to various authors including Raymond Lully or Johannes de Rupescissa.</note>. From this one can gather that it is completed sooner at one time than at another; likewise, in one place sooner than in another; and also, by one artist sooner than by another. For there are two things that either further or hinder the **Work**: just as there are two things that complete it or destroy it, namely the skill of the **operator** <term>operator</term> <note>original: *Laboranten*</note> and the virtue of the **celestial influence** <term>celestial influence</term> <note>original: *influenz*</note>. For one master is more skillful, of a more subtle understanding, and more diligent and cautious in practice than another. Therefore, he who chooses a better root, prepares more suitable vessels and **instruments** <term>instruments</term> <note>original: *Instrumenta*</note> for it, can provide a more moderate **regulation** <term>regulation</term> <note>original: *Regiment*; the careful management of heat over time</note>, thinks more diligently by comparing causes against **effects** <term>effects</term> <note>original: *effectis*</note>, chooses a better location, and obeys God and the Saints with a more fervent spirit—he can proceed all the sooner. 

Therefore, the artist is commanded to do two things: Firstly, that he honor God the Almighty with vows and a pure heart, so that He may enlighten him with high understanding and clear away from his Work all hindrances thrown in the way by the Devil, our adversary, which can occur in countless numbers. Secondly, however, that he frequently walk around the vessels and diligently observe the colors seen and the many forms of Nature, and grasp the miraculous works of Nature and of God with their causes, **effects** <term>effects</term>, and signs, so that from this he knows how to conduct himself in the **regulation** <term>regulation</term> and how to prevent dangers and misfortune.

Hence ***The Lily*** says: The **Philosophers** have set unequal **terms** <note>original: *terminos*; referring to the time limits or durations of the stages.</note> for this burning or roasting, perhaps because of the inequality of the moist and dripping compared to the dry; for in the moist, it is **solidified** <term>solidified</term> <note>original: *coaguliert*</note> more quickly, and in the dry, more slowly, as **Astanus** <note>original: *Astanus*; likely referring to Ostanes, a legendary Persian magus and alchemist.</note> says. Hold to what **Hermes** <note>original: *Hermete*; Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> says: that the Work should be repeated and rubbed for so long, with cooking in **manure** <note>original: *mist*; refers to *venter equinum* (horse dung), which provided a steady, gentle, low heat for digestion.</note>, until it becomes visible, just as the transformation of the Work will teach you.

...afterward, this same **composition** <term>composition</term> <note>original: *Cōposition*; the mixture of alchemical substances.</note> shall be increased anew with its **milk** <note>original: *milch*; often referring to the "mercurial milk" or the white liquid used to nourish the growing Stone.</note> and let it drink as much as it can drink. And this is the **Oil of the Philosophers** <term>Oil of the Philosophers</term>, which transforms **Mercury** <term>mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurium*</note> and the imperfect metals into the very best mineral gold. And thus it is not unfairly compared to the **birth of a human** <note>The alchemists frequently used the "microcosm" of human biology to explain the "macrocosm" of chemical creation.</note>, as **Morienus** <term>Morienus</term> <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who allegedly taught the secrets of the Art to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says in his dialogue with **Khalid** <note>original: *Castrensi*; referring to the *Liber de compositione alchimiae*, a dialogue between Morienus and King Khalid (Calid).</note>. 

For first is the **intercourse** <note>original: *Coitus*</note>, which is the **dissolution** <note>original: *Solutio*</note> of the seed—namely, when the Mercury drips down from the heat. Second is **conception** <note>original: *empfēgnus*</note>, when the **Body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note> is dissolved by the water. Third is **pregnancy** <note>original: *schwengerung*</note>, when the **seeds** <note>original: *Spermata*</note> mix together, and this happens in 40 days. Fourth is **birth** <note>original: *geburt*</note>, namely, when the **Soul** <note>original: *Seel*</note> is poured in and reaches perfect whiteness, which according to some happens in 70 days. Fifth is **nourishment** <note>original: *narung*</note>, when it is strengthened and empowered toward redness and stability. Therefore, the **Stone** <note>original: *Lapis*</note> is born in whiteness, but in redness, it is fed and fully nourished to a masculine strength.

Colors, however, that follow one after another, indicate the transformation of the natures and forms. Therefore, our **Stone** <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical work.</note> transforms itself before it is made perfect through **Art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy itself.</note>, from one nature into another, from one color into another: and often a destruction occurs, and often a birth. It contains within itself many different and contrary effects and also takes on many different names; and unequal workings occur in one thing, which nevertheless—because they strive toward a single **goal** <note>original: *Termino*</note>—are also called a single Work. Therefore, when one considers the end, it is a single work: but if one looks at the inequality of the effects, there is a distinction of workings.

Therefore, the **sublimation** <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: *sublimation*; in alchemy, this refers to heating a substance until it rises as a vapor and then solidifies again, purified.</note> is a single work. For **Alphidius** <note>An Arabic alchemical author often cited in medieval texts.</note> and **Saturnus** say: our meaning of the entire Work is nothing else than that one should take the Stone which is well known to us, and called **Adrap** <note>An Arabic term for the material of the stone, often associated with lead.</note> in Arabic, but called **Lead** <note>original: *Plumbum*</note> in Latin—and it is the Stone of the Philosophers and has very great virtues above all stones—and put it into the philosophical vessel to sublimate; and sublimate it so long until it reaches the extreme purification of sublimation. And this is the first and true working. **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> also places the entire Art in sublimation and speaks the truth. For this **philosophical sublimation** is not a common sublimation, but rather encompasses within itself all these seven workings:

The first is **purification**, so that you take the purest substance.
The second is **solution** <note>original: *Solutio*</note>, that you dissolve the entire matter into a water.
The third is **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: *Putrefaction*; a stage of rotting or decay believed to be necessary for new life to emerge.</note>, for nothing is born unless it first rots. Therefore, one should putrefy it so that, being thus cooked, they can be better separated.
The fourth is the **washing**, for a foul thing must be washed from its destructive impurity. In this Art, however, washing, **inceration** <note>The process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency.</note>, purification, mixing, and **constitution** <note>original: *Complexion*</note> are all one thing.
The fifth is **coagulation** <note>original: *Coagulatio*</note>, for one must gently dry out the water in the sun with the earth and coagulate it so that it is turned into a powder or dust.
The sixth working is **calcination** <term>calcination</term> <note>original: *Calcination*; reducing a substance to a powder through high heat.</note>, for a calcined thing is more suitable for sublimation and is closer to stability. And this is called **fusion** <note>original: *fusio*</note> or casting and unchangeability by many **Philosophers**.
And all these **operations** occur in the single sublimation.

And therefore, he who can sublimate correctly can complete the entire work. Therefore, sublimation is a separation of the coarse parts from the most subtle, or the **unfixed** <note>Volatile substances that evaporate easily.</note> from the **stable** <note>Fixed substances that resist the fire.</note>. For the unstable parts rise up through the mist or smoke. And one must watch carefully that they do not fly away, but are instead made stable with the fixed parts. And they remain there for the reason that they give a "flow" to the coarser parts and protect them from **vitrification** <note>original: *gläsung*; the undesirable turning of the material into useless glass due to excessive heat.</note>. Now, through these seven **dispositions**...

...found in the **sublimation** <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind.</note>, every intelligent person can reach the perfection of the work. Therefore, do not be negligent in the **Purification** which is accomplished through sublimation. For whatever the quality of the purification may be, a corresponding perfection will follow upon it.

From this it is understood that the Sublimation of the **Stone** <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher’s Stone.</note> is called **refining** <note>original: *affinatio*</note>, namely, so that it may be elevated in substance, virtue, and color. Therefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says in the *Turba*:
> He who knows how to separate the airy from the watery, and the watery from the earthy dryness, and how to join together the purest parts—that is, the airy, spiritual, and most subtle parts—and make from them a **Medicine**, he is a true seeker of this perfect mastery.

And thus (as **Geber** <note>An influential 8th-century Arabic alchemist, often called the "Father of Chemistry."</note> says) we make the imperfect perfect in our **Magistery** <term>Magistery</term> <note>The "Masterwork" or the completed alchemical process.</note>, by itself, without the addition of any external thing. And in this, we purify these separated parts in the best way: through **Digestion** <term>Digestion</term> <note>A process of slow, gentle heating, similar to incubation.</note> and cooking we make them subtle, and we unite the refined parts, making them perfect with the very highest virtues and colors through constancy, until from them comes the purest and most subtle **Tincture** <term>Tincture</term> <note>The potent liquid produced at the end of the work, capable of "dyeing" or transforming base metals.</note> which shall penetrate the imperfect bodies and transform them into the noblest Gold, as **Hamis** <note>Possibly a reference to an Arabic authority or a variation of a name like Ahmad.</note> in the *Turba* wishes. 

And this is the characteristic of sublimating, which comes to this perfection of the stone not all at once, but through **degrees** <note>original: *Gradus*</note> and steps. For the Stone shall gradually reach the highest degree of perfection through Sublimation. ...simultaneously three Regimens: likewise four, and thus of each one in particular. But there is no need to use many words now. For when our Matter is in our vessel and our Matter feels our Sun <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" often represents the heating element or the active "sulfur" within the chemicals themselves.</note>, it will immediately be dissolved into a water. This same water, however, leaps up to the head of the vessel through the smoke—that is, through the wind or air. And afterward, it descends again to the bottom of the vessel and dissolves the Matter, and the rest gradually becomes a water. And thus the sublimation and solution of the Stone occur simultaneously; and both things—namely, the rising and the falling—are called **Dissolution** <term>Dissolutio</term> <note>original: *Dissolutio*; the chemical breakdown of a solid into a liquid state, often seen as the first major step of the work.</note>.

Thereafter it begins to thicken and turns into an Earth; and gradually the Earth that stood above the water settles to the bottom of the vessel and becomes black and stinking; and then it is called **Putrefaction** <term>Putrefactio</term> <note>original: *Putrefactio*; the stage of decay and blackness, historically known as the *nigredo*, which signifies the death of the old forms.</note>. But after a long time, through the warmth of the Sun and the washing of the water, the black earth loses its color and the stinking smell. And then it is called **Ablution** <term>Ablutio</term> <note>original: *Ablutio*; the process of "washing" the matter through repeated distillation to remove impurities.</note> and purification. After that, however, the water is diminished, and the earth is dried out by the tempered Sun; and then it is called **Ceration** <term>Ceratio</term> <note>original: *Ceratio*; the process of softening the matter until it has the consistency of wax (*cera*), allowing it to melt without evaporating.</note>. For then the entire Matter is turned into an Earth, if you know how to operate correctly.

And in this consists the entire Regimen: namely, that it be turned into an earth. But when the entire Matter is turned into a strong, standing earth that cannot be poured, it is then called **Congelation** <term>Congelatio</term> <note>original: *Congelatio*; the solidification or "freezing" of the substance into a stable form.</note>; and up until this time, one must act very cautiously, for in this resides, as it were, the entire power of the Regimen. Therefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure considered the father of alchemy.</note> says: "Its power is complete when it is changed into an earth." For the entire Mastery is nothing other than making a right Solution and a perfect Congelation. 

The congealed Matter, however, being perfectly dried out through greater cooking by the Sun, begins to turn white and to flow like a white oil; and then it is called **Calcination** <term>Calcinatio</term> <note>original: *Calcinatio*; the reduction of a substance to a fine powder or white state through prolonged heat.</note>. And when it reaches perfect whiteness—such that this whiteness surpasses all other whiteness—it is then called **Whitening** <term>Dealbatio</term> <note>original: *Dealbatio*; the attainment of the "White Stone," which can transform base metals into silver.</note>; and then the **Stone** <term>Lapis</term> <note>original: *Lapis*; the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is perfected in its whiteness.

### CHAPTER XXIV.
### That the knowledge of colors is necessary to rightly govern our Regimen.

The various colors indicate an inequality of the cookings <note>original: *kochungen*; the alchemical process of "digestion" or sustained heating in the vessel.</note>. But in every natural and artificial thing, there are various colors according to the inequality of the cooking / so long as the thing is in motion / and on the path of generation. Yet every thing has its own and natural color / when it is in the fulfillment of its final cooking / as one sees in flowers / fruits / wood, and animals. Therefore, because the **Philosophers' Stone** <term>Lapis Philosophorum</term> is guided through long art / and goes through many cookings / it is also changed with countless colors. But since it is a thing of art and of nature / it is now ended with its own color. And because it is made not just so that it *is*, but so that it may be for something else / according to the end for which it is made / so must its color be determined. It is, however, made for Gold. Gold is **citrine red** <note>original: *Citrin rot*; a deep golden-orange or saffron color considered the mark of the perfected Work.</note>, therefore [the Stone] will also necessarily receive a citrine red color. And because it is not made so that Gold becomes of it / but that it makes Gold out of other metals—and since other metals have a great difference from Gold in their colors / and when a thing that is colored is mixed with another / both colors are changed / and the lesser hinders the greater / and one does not obtain the color one desires / unless a more specific color far surpasses the others. And from this it is necessarily concluded that before all things the Artist must foreknow the specific and natural color / which the **Elixir** <note>A potent substance, often synonymous here with the Stone, used to transform base metals.</note> should have / and that he know beforehand / what the final state shall be in the completion. SECOND PART CHAPTER XXVI.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

# That the second work in the regimen is Putrefaction.

Bodies that are not **dissolved** <term>solviert</term> <note>original: "solviert"; referring to the process of turning a solid into a liquid state.</note> are also not made **subtle**. Therefore, you must work patiently in the **dissolution** <term>solutio</term> of the Stone, making the coarser parts subtle and separating the subtle from the coarse, until the entire **body** <term>corpus</term> becomes subtle, spiritual, and volatile. This, however, as has been said, occurs through the **Mercury** <term>Quecksilber</term> which is airy; it dissolves the body and gradually draws out its **souls** <term>animae</term> and carries them with it into **Heaven** <note>In alchemical laboratory practice, "Heaven" refers to the upper part or "head" of the glass still where vapors collect.</note>, and through this, its virtue is constantly increased by the cooperation of the **fire's** heat. Therefore, it finally dissolves and overcomes the entire body and carries it with it into the **air**.

But before it brings the body to such perfection, it is necessary that it first dissolve the body into a water and, in dissolving it, **putrefy** it <note>Putrefaction, or *putrefactio*, is the stage where the matter rots and turns black, signaling the death of the old form.</note>. Therefore, the first method of dissolution is to putrefy and rot the matter. For putrefaction begins at the same time as the start of the dissolution: but the **putrefaction** is not yet fulfilled when the entire matter is dissolved into a water, but is fulfilled afterward; and in this putrefaction, the **Stone** <term>lapis</term> is dissolved even better than it was dissolved before. For the longer and more steadily one operates and works, the more subtle the Stone becomes.

Therefore, the entire **Mastery** <term>magisterium</term> <note>The complete alchemical process or "Great Work."</note> consists in putrefaction. For if it does not rot, nothing will come of it. Upon putrefaction follows the **blackness** <note>The *nigredo* stage, often symbolized by a crow's head.</note> and within this, the moisture. The cause, however, that moves the matter to putrefaction is the **tempered heat**. Therefore, **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher often cited in alchemical texts.</note> says: When heat works into the moisture, it gives birth to a blackness. Therefore, these three follow one after another: moisture, decay, and blackness. Hence **Artephius** <note>A legendary alchemical author, likely a pseudonym for a 12th-century writer.</note> says: The **glass house** <note>The alchemical flask or vessel.</note> should stand in a subtle position until the enclosed moist matter gradually becomes rotten and black.

It is therefore first to be noted that putrefaction is necessary in the Stone: for no **birth** occurs except after **destruction**, and a thing is not improved unless its form is first entirely and utterly destroyed. We desire, however, to bring the Stone to a perfect form of an **elixir**. Therefore, it must first be destroyed and corrupted.

<summary>This page explains that after the initial dissolution of the "body," the matter must undergo "putrefaction" (symbolic decay and blackening) to destroy its old form before it can be reborn as the Elixir. This stage, driven by gentle heat, is described as the essential foundation of the entire Great Work.</summary>

Therefore, in Aries, the entire matter should be transformed into a uniform substance. And in this, no one should go astray, for the entire secret lies in the beginning of the work, namely in the **putrefaction**.

Secondly, note that this **putrefaction** is a perfect and universal mixing of two bodies. Therefore, in the *Book of Miserula* <term>libro Miserula</term> it is said: **Sol** <term>Sol</term> <note>The Sun, representing the masculine principle or gold.</note>, which is of the same nature as **Luna** <term>Luna</term> <note>The Moon, representing the feminine principle or silver.</note>, must drink, and she will become full; and she shall drink abundantly of the water of **Luna**, and sleep together in friendship, and be mixed through the smallest parts. For one nature delights in another because of the similarity of their natures. Then the seed—that is, the "fatness" of the Sun—goes into the **Lunar body** <term>Corpus Lunare</term>, and is mixed through the smallest parts, and joined together by a general mixing; and through this, the Moon or **Luna** becomes pregnant, which occurs in 40 days. If no such mixing occurs, no birth follows afterward, as **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist who supposedly taught the art to the King of Egypt.</note> says. And if no pregnancy occurs, there will be no giving of birth.

Thirdly, note that there are three signs of **putrefaction**: namely, the blackness, the foul smell, and the subtlety of the powder, so that it is nearly impalpable. For the fire, together with the moisture, makes the Stone black during its preparation. And this blackness is a sign of a perfect mixing and the acceptance of one by the other, as is said in the *Assembly of Philosophers* <term>Turba</term>.

Just as the **solution** <term>Solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note> happens through the Mercury <note>original: "Quecksilber".</note>, so too do the **putrefaction** and blackening; for it is moist, and when one moisture is mixed with another, it **putrefies** <term>putreficierts</term> and makes it "fat" and black. ...stinking in smell and subtle in spirit. Therefore, it is said in the *Lily* <term>Lilio</term> <note>Likely referring to the *Lilium Philosophorum*, a popular alchemical treatise.</note>: "As long as the same blackness lasts, the woman <note>In alchemy, the "woman" often represents Mercury or the volatile, feminine principle.</note> rules—that is, until the whiteness—and the moisture of the Mercury is destructive." And Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit-alchemist.</note> says in the new translation: "Our whole Mastery <term>Magisterium</term> is nothing other than an extraction of water from the earth, and the pouring of that same water back over the earth until it rots. For this water rots with the water." And Raymond <note>Ramon Lull.</note> says in *On Terms* <term>de terminis</term>: "Until the entire matter becomes black." Gallinarius says: "Until the matter at the bottom shall be black." And Johannes Teb. <note>Likely referring to an alchemical author such as Johannes de Tecena.</note> says: "The black color is a sign of corruption or destruction, which is praiseworthy."

The smell is also a sign of perfect **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction</term>, but not just any smell: rather, a completely vile and unbearable stench. For the **solution** <term>Solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> and putrefaction begin with an evil stink, which grows steadily until it reaches its peak; it is therefore called a "deadly poison" in the *Book of Saturn* <note>Saturn is traditionally associated with lead and the color black (Nigredo).</note>—namely before the putrefaction—and it kills human bodies, and afterwards the metallic bodies. This smell, however, is perceived more by the intellect than by the nose. For how it exists within the Work, we have learned through experience before the Work. One must take great care within the Work not to actually sense its smell; for the putrefaction is not completed as long as one can still perceive its odor.

This twofold property of the **Stone** <term>Lapis</term> is expressed through the metaphor of a dead man. For it is said in the *Lily* that the Stone requires a gentle fire from the beginning, and that it looks like a dead man for several days, like a man in his grave. In the same place, Theophilus says: "The belly of that same woman is full of water and full of poison." Therefore, it is said:

> It finally grows stiff and pours forth foul odors. <note>original: "Rigescit demum, & olidos effundit odores."</note>

The third sign of a perfect putrefaction is a powder that cannot be felt or grasped, which must be tested not by touch but by sight. And this is as much as to say that it should be like a black oil or like a reddish blood, so that the whole or at least the greatest part of the matter is uniformly black and should not cling together, but rather be separated from itself. And Theophilus also says of this: "Make a grave for that same **Dragon** <term>Drachen</term> <note>The Dragon often symbolizes the raw, volatile matter or the "Philosophical Mercury" that must be tamed.</note>, and bury the woman in it with him until he is turned into blood."

Fourthly, note that this blackness precedes the whiteness. For it is said in the *Lily*, where the whiteness and redness are discussed: neither happens without blackness, for the blackness is encountered first in the Work. And they indicate that this is the **first key** <term>schlieissel</term> of the Work.

# CHAPTER XXVII.

## That the third work in the Regimen is the Whitening.

The Philosophers say, however, that this *Corpus* <note>The "Body" or material substance of the Work.</note>, having been thus blackened, is dead. Therefore *Gallinarius* says: This dissolution of the black body we also call a "dissolution of the dead," and it usually happens in 40 days. Therefore it is necessary that one washes it so that it becomes clean, and afterward makes it alive, so that it receives its life and virtue <note>In this context, "virtue" means the inherent power or medicinal property of the substance.</note> again. For the *Rosarius* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* text itself.</note> says: change the Stone into something better and not into something worse. It is changed into something better when it becomes a **Composite Elixir**. But it is changed into something worse when it is destroyed. For in that case, there is a loss and no gain. Therefore the <term>Lapis</term> <note>The Stone.</note> is destroyed and corrupted, not so that it should remain dead, but so that it comes to a better nature and greater virtue through the cooking.

And therefore it is said in the *Treatise Miserula*: In the first work, a blackness appears; but both bodies are washed by the water that rises through <term>Sublimation</term> <note>The process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a solid, used here as a purifying "washing."</note>, and when it falls down again, they are clarified and made alive; afterward, they will be of the greatest whiteness, like a shining marble stone and like the whitest salt. And then it makes **Silver** <note>original: "Lunam," literally "the Moon," the alchemical name for silver.</note> from all bodies. That happens, however, when she is "married"—that is, when they are mixed in the vessel through the smallest parts and [merged] into one nature through the [power] of the

And for this reason, warm water washes away more than cold. Just as wax is made white by the dew and warmth, but flax is bleached through moisture and the sun. And this is the reason why after the rotting of the stone, one must keep the fire steady until it becomes white. For through the steady fire, the earth is <term>calcined</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter and reduce it to a powder.</note> and rubbed, and as it continues, it is gradually divided, and therefore it finally becomes white. In which whitening the water co-operates, which is constantly pressed into the earth and rises into the heights through the heat; indeed, it becomes much more incorporated and embodied with the earth. Therefore **Ignotus** <note>An "Unknown" author or authority.</note> has said: Rub it often with its water and calcine it often, until through the washing of the water and fire all uncleanness comes away from it. The other whitening is this: the <term>putrefied</term> <note>The matter that has undergone decomposition or rotting.</note> matter remains below in the vessel; although some subtle and airy **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> always rise with a watery vapor into the heights of the vessel through the dissolving warmth. The matter is like water or black oil, still coarse and heavy, impure and put together or mixed from body, spirit, and soul. But the Art that desires to make an **Elixir** <note>The perfected substance capable of transmutation and healing.</note> from it seeks how it may make the same subtle, and <term>tinge</term> <note>to dye or transform the nature and color of the matter.</note> it with a perfect color and make it stable. This, however, cannot happen if it does not separate the subtle from the coarse, and in turn, through the subtle, make the coarse subtle.

...[the student] <note>The OCR begins with "lers," likely the end of the German word "Schülers" (student's) from the previous page.</note> perceives and understands that he sees it with his eyes, even though an inequality appears to him. For always, after the **solution** <term>solution: the process of dissolving a solid into liquid state</term> of the **Stone** <note>original: "Steins"</note>, something flies above and a part remains below as long as the Stone is **unfixed** <term>unfixed: volatile; a substance that evaporates or changes easily when heated</term>. And that which rises always takes something bodily with it into the air, and that which remains below always drinks the rising water. For just as much descends as that which rises. Thus they are moved in the circle of their **sphere** <note>original: "Sphæræ"</note> by the heat which drives up from below and lifts the steamy vapors, and by the cold which, from above, constricts and presses them down. But that which descends goes immediately into the **body** <note>original: "corpus"</note> and gradually makes it volatile. For the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus"</note> is subtle and, by its fiery nature, sharp.

From this it happens that, although a **black earth** <note>The "black earth" refers to the *nigredo* stage, the initial state of decomposition in the alchemical work.</note> is seen lying at the bottom of the vessel from the beginning of the **extraction** <note>original: "extractiō"</note>, yet after some time it is at last entirely dispersed and made subtle through the softening of the water and the grinding of the fire. It rises entirely into the air and is carried away with the spirit—not all at once, but gradually—until they become entirely one body and one spirit. From this follows the whole, which possesses one virtue, one color, and one property. Thereafter, however, the whole **sublimated** <term>sublimation: heating a substance to turn it into vapor, which then cools back into a purified solid</term> matter is **fixed** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> at the bottom through constant precipitation and made steady, yet gradually, until nothing more rises.

And then the spirit is converted into a body, and yet the body does not lose the virtue of the spirit. For because the spirits have been made entirely subtle, the whole body also remains subtle: for it is a thing that is of the nature of the **quintessence** <note>original: "quintæ essentiæ"; the "fifth essence," a pure, celestial substance beyond the four earthly elements.</note>. The spirits were also quite clear and transparent; therefore, the body is as well. They were entirely pure; therefore, the body is also of the greatest purity. They were quite white; therefore, the body is also entirely white, and so forth. But one must not think that as soon as the body rests at the bottom it is steady enough or ready for the **white tincture** <term>tincture: a potent alchemical liquid or powder capable of transforming and coloring other substances</term>, unless the whole that was sublimated rests steadily at the bottom and pours like a shining oil. In whatever way or at whatever time this happens, it is certain that the spirit, body, and **soul** <note>original: "anima"</note> are most perfectly united, and a total friendship is made between the warm and cold, the moist and dry.

Of this manner of **governance** <note>original: "Regiments"; in alchemy, "regimen" refers to the specific method of managing the heat and the stages of the work.</note> **Morienus** <note>Morienus: A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit known for his dialogues on the philosopher's stone.</note> speaks when he says:

> If you do not perfectly purify the body and do not dry it, nor have whitened it well, and have not mixed the soul into the same, and taken away all its stench, until after its purification the tincture falls into it, then you have accomplished nothing in this mastery.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

### That the Rule of our Stone in the
### Conjunction of Spirit and Body
### is Divine.

This Art is called "Divine" because of one part of its rule <note>the "regiment" or sequence of operations</note> which is above nature and above human understanding, as all the philosophers say. This same Divine rule, however, occurs at the time of whitening, namely when the joining of the soul, the spirits, and the bodies—which were once enemies—takes place. For this conjunction <term>conjunction: the "alchemical marriage" where opposing elements like spirit (volatile) and body (solid) are permanently united</term> <note>original: "coniunction"</note> relies upon the protection of God. 

It happens quickly: namely, that the medicine coagulates the quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum viuum"</note>—not common mercury, but the mercury of the Stone. If it were not coagulated in its origin with that same medicine of which Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "Father of Chemistry"</note> speaks, it would fly away <note>evaporate</note> along with the entire medicine. For Geber does not speak there of common mercury <note>original: "Quecksilber"</note>, though the words may appear so; rather, he speaks of the mercury that is coagulated and stable for the Elixir. 

Therefore, from the beginning, there must be only one material in which the virtue of the body, spirit, and soul <note>original: "animæ"</note> exists, much like a mineral medicine that needs no other external thing as an aid. Instead, it has within itself everything it requires for the working of its rule, whether for sublimation <term>sublimation: heating a substance to a gas and back to a solid to purify it</term>, or for fixation <term>fixation: making a substance stable so it no longer evaporates or changes in heat</term>, or for melting, or for congelation <term>congelation: the thickening or "freezing" of a liquid into a solid</term>, or the like. For the *Lilium* <note>likely referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae*, a famous alchemical text</note> says: It is only one thing that has within itself a body, soul, and spirit, which tint <note>transform or color the metal</note> all at once.

in whose operation no other helper is necessary. Each of the aforementioned bodies and spirits, when made perfect through preparation <note>original: "praeparation"</note>, is a ready white and red elixir <term>Elixir: a medicinal or transformative substance, here the final alchemical goal</term> <note>original: "Elixir"</note> by itself alone. Also, the beautiful dispute that Rhazes sets between Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note> and Gold shows that they mean for the entire Stone to be Mercurial, yet in its hidden Gold it possesses the Sulfur <term>Sulfur: in alchemy, the active, masculine principle of combustion and color, often paired with Mercury</term> <note>original: "Sulphur"</note>. From which it is understood that the Philosophers' Stone <note>original: "Lapis Philosophorum"</note> is solely a Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, for it is entirely a volatile spirit. And therefore, although Mercury takes the place of a woman in the composition of the elixir <note>original: "Elixiris"</note>, its first entire operation is like that of the man; and this remains so as long as it is volatile, and as long as it is held by the body, which is the coagulated Sulfur <note>original: "coagulierte Sulphur"</note>. This body <note>original: "corpus"</note>, however, is not added to it from elsewhere, but it possesses it within its own nature potentially <note>original: "potestate"</note>; it is, however, brought into actuality <note>original: "actum"</note> when, through suitable digestion <term>Digestion: the process of slow, gentle heating to mature a substance</term> <note>original: "digestion"</note>, it receives the property and nature of a body. And then it is called a body by itself alone. Therefore it also happens in all operations of metals and minerals, that generally every composition occurs solely from the spirits and their own vapors, whether they be simple or mixed. These are called spirits beforehand because of their volatility in heat; but at the end of the "cooking" <note>the alchemical heating process</note>, they are made stable by the cold, and are made permanent by themselves with their hidden bodies which are within them potentially <note>original: "potestate"</note>, without the addition of any external body. And this is of the nature of earthly spirits, for the heavy elements <note>original: "Element"</note> are a cause of stability: especially the Earth, into which one can only press with difficulty, but it afterwards holds it firmly; it accepts the impression more easily, however, when water is mixed with it. Therefore it is manifest that the mineral spirits are also composed of the four elements, and both the heavy and the light are vaporous from the boiling heat: for in this way the light elements carry the heavy ones mixed with them into the heights; and

### SECOND PART CHAPTER XXIII.

Yet the heavy elements among these do not lose their nature entirely, nor the quality of their nature. For otherwise, they could not pass from the physical to the spiritual state, which is however false. For the bodies <note>original: "corpora"</note> are spirits in potential <note>original: "potestate"</note>. Thus, in these too, there is a spirit <note>original: "spiritus"</note> from which the elixir <term>Elixir: the final transformative substance of the alchemical process</term> is made. For since the heavy elements are the cause of fixation <term>Fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand fire</term> when they are finally cooked and purified, they possess the virtue of both a body and a spirit. They are nevermore separated from the light elements, for the light are contained within the heavy, just as a single thing contains within itself all four elements—both the active and the passive—and everything necessary for the birth of an elixir. 

Thus now our Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>, purified from its uncleanness and through the appropriate fire, is a simple volatile spirit in actuality <note>original: "spiritus actu"</note>, and is a body in its most immediate potential <note>original: "corpus in potestate propinquissima"</note>. It is therefore necessary that we bring it into a body in actuality <note>original: "corpus actu"</note>, and then it is also the solar body of the Philosophers <note>original: "corpus solare Philosophorum"</note>, and a tincture <term>Tincture: a substance capable of "dyeing" or transforming the nature of a metal</term>, and the Gold of the Philosophers <note>original: "aurum Philosophorum"</note>, and the lead that overflows <note>original: "das bley / das ers/öll"; likely referring to the "oil of the ore," a liquid state of the metal</note>.

And this Gold is a ferment <term>Ferment: a substance, like yeast, that triggers a transformation in a larger mass</term> for both tinctures, the white and the red. But quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum viuum"</note> is a ferment, and of this the Philosophers say: "The ferment of gold is gold, just as the ferment of dough is dough." They do not say, however, that the ferment of silver is silver, for all ferments and all fixations occur through Gold and not through silver. 

And for this reason Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: "No metal falls into Mercury [to be transformed] except Gold." Of which quicksilver Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: "That the white smoke is the tincture of the deceased bodies." If the white smoke were not there, alchemical gold could in no way be made.

And in this way it happens that the tincture and the mixing of the body <note>original: "corporis"</note> and spirit <note>original: "spiritus"</note> occur simultaneously. For that which is dry is thin; therefore, it becomes firm through moisture. But the moist receives a strong impression and imprint from the dry. For moisture alone receives an impression quickly but also lets it go quickly; but dryness alone receives an impression with difficulty and slowly, yet it lets go of what is received with difficulty. But when they are both tempered together at the same time, they receive a strong impression and are also stable in the fire. For the moist protects the dry from combustibility, and the dry protects the moist from flowing. Therefore, the fire has a free dominion over both of them for itself. But the air, because it is warm and moist, makes the earth and the water clear, so that they may be stretched and poured. The Fire, however, makes the entire compound <term>Compositum: the combined alchemical substance</term> red, strengthens it, and makes it mature. For it causes the air to mix through the subtle parts.

It also makes the water hard and stable with the earth, and therefore assigns to it a stable tincture.

From this, understand now that the heavy elements help and work more toward stability and rest than the light ones. The light ones, however, help more with the flow of the tinctures; nevertheless, they all work toward all things. Especially, however, the fire does not work toward fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term> because of its active, penetrating virtue, and because it carries others with it and dries them out; therefore, the first cause of fixation is the earth, for it is more stable than all the other elements. Next is the water, for it is closer to tempering the earth, and with its coldness, it protects against combustibility.

Thus, understand what was said—that Fire does not enter into the White Elixir—as referring to its primary character. For all four elements are indeed present in it, yet the power and effect of Fire are not as great as in the Red Elixir, to which Fire is specifically assigned. This Fire is a red sulfur, not added from the outside, but drawn out from within.

Take this as the foundation of your knowledge: in the operation of the Elixir, the "tender Nature" (which is called the "body" <note>original: "corpus"</note>), even when mixed with a very subtle spirit and sublimated alongside it, remains the immediate cause of coagulation <term>coagulation: the process by which a gaseous or liquid substance becomes solid</term> and fixation <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</term>. This is true even if it is not visible to the elements. From this nature, combined with the watery substance, comes the origin of the sulfur and the ferment <term>ferment: a substance, like yeast in bread, that transforms the entire alchemical mass into its own nature</term>. This fixed Nature exists in all things composed of the four elements, to the extent that they are refined and brought into a spiritual state—sometimes in actuality <note>original: "in actu"</note>, and sometimes in potentiality <note>original: "in potestate"</note>. Therefore, they contain everything within themselves by which they are made stable, provided they do not flee from the heat.

External fire, administered through the alchemical art as mentioned above, works primarily toward this fixation. If this fire is too weak, it hinders stability because it retains the original moisture rather than consuming it. It is from this moisture, however, that the Stone <note>original: "Lapis"</note> primarily gains its "flow" or fluidity. From this, learn once more which element predominates in each stage of the process <term>regiment: a specific stage or "rule" in the alchemical process governed by a particular planet or quality</term>. At the beginning, the Stone is cold and moist; at the end, it appears warm and dry to the eyes. Yet, according to the understanding, it is actually warm and moist—entirely balanced and tempered, just as gold is. You must therefore recognize how much each quality of the elements increases or decreases.

...sulfur <note>original: "phur", completing "Sulphur" from the previous page</note> participated in both Natures: or where there were nothing in this thing that could bring the Sun <note>original: "Solem"</note> and the Moon <note>original: "Lunam"</note> to the common Nature and color of Quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti viui"</note>. Therefore, although in our Stone, Sun and Moon are distinct—as far as location, properties, and color are concerned, as is evident from what was said before—nevertheless, because they are related Natures, one is easily transformed into the other. Therefore, Hermes says: "There will never be any true red tincture without the Red Stone." For the white alone, without the Red Stone, would not tinge into a perfect redness. But since the Moon holds the first dominion and transforms the Sun into herself by giving him her nature, color, and property—therefore, even if she already has more of the Nature of Mercury (because the sulfur is volatile), she is also not unjustly called the ferment of the White Elixir. Nevertheless, both ferments from both bodies are more noble within the Sun. For both bodies, because of the kinship of their Natures—having sprung from one Father and one Mother—are transformed into a primary Nature of Mercury through change. Afterward, from that same thing—that is, from their hidden interior—two sulfuric ferments can be drawn: first a white one, and then a red one. 

For it is not actually called a "ferment" until the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> is coagulated with it and is tinged into a form of Gold or Silver. From the beginning, however, nothing is called a ferment unless it is first a Material from which the ferment is drawn. Thus, the Sun primarily gives the perfection and completeness of the Stone, and the final completion; and from it comes the soul <note>original: "anima"</note> and the tingeing sulfur. And the spirit of Mercury <note>original: "spiritus Mercurii"</note>, which comes from the Moon, is what sharpens and impregnates, and finally draws it to its Nature and color. And this is what is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Azoth <note>The essential transformative agent, often identified with Mercury</note> cannot essentially take the color of Laton <note>original: "Latoni"; a term for unrefined or "black" metal</note>, nor transform it."

### THE NEW ROSARY
### (ROSARII NOVI)

But gold cannot become silver unless it is first destroyed; and when it is destroyed, it becomes black. There is, however, no path from the black to the citrine-red <note>A yellowish-orange color stage in alchemy, often occurring between the white and red phases</note> except through the white, just as there is no transition from the citrine-red to the white unless it first becomes black. Citrine-red is nothing other than a variation of the blackness. For when heat acts upon moisture, it first causes blackness; but when it acts upon dryness and continues steadily, it causes citrine-red. And for this reason, the <term>Lilium: an influential alchemical text, often titled 'Lilium Intelligentiae' or 'The Lily of Intelligence'</term> says: where the bodies are not divided, the colors of the souls do not appear. And further down it is said: The spirit and the soul are not joined with the body in the proper way except in the white color. For then all colors that can be imagined in the world appear, and then they are confirmed into one color; that is, they come together in the white. The whitening, however, is the beginning and the foundation of the whole Work; and it is no longer changed into many colors (those which are truly colors) except into the red, in which is the final end. In the cooking after the white, one arrives at the citrine-red by increasing the fire in the governance <note>The 'regiment' or controlled application of heat</note>, and after the white, you can never go wrong. Therefore, <term>Mireris: a legendary or pseudonymous alchemical authority often cited in medieval anthologies</term> says: One must first bury the earth in a **piece of Egyptian cloth** <note>original: "petia panni Egyptii"; likely referring to a specific method of filtration or a symbolic stage of concealment</note>; after that, one must make the compound white, so that it finally becomes the **tingeing sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur tingirende"; sulfur that has the power to color or transmute other metals</note> and becomes stable, and after that becomes red. For it becomes black twice, citrine-colored twice, and red twice. But the second red tinges, which is not made except through the first whitening; if you wish to work philosophically—that is, if you whiten with foresight—you will be blessed. But if you see this happen quickly, a great terror will come upon you. And therefore, **Raymond of the Borders** <note>original: "Raymundus de terminis"; referring to Raymond Lull, a famous philosopher and alchemist</note> says: After the **putrefaction** <note>the stage of decay where the matter breaks down and turns black</note>, you must make the sulfur, whose determined (**critical**) <note>original: "cretici"</note> days are 90 at most; after that, no one can go wrong anymore.

Therefore, you should know thirdly that after the completion of the white, you should proceed to the perfect red. For the redness of the Medicine must be perfect, as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of alchemy</note> says, which happens in this way: after the incombustible sulfur of the two aforementioned bodies has been made white, that same sulfur is made red through a greater cooking of the fire. For thus, gold is made out of silver. And thus the white and red sulfur, as the *Rosarius* says, are from one material of the metals, yet cooked in various ways. And **Plato** says: In every silver there is red sulfur, and such sulfur is in the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>original: "Sole vnnd Luna"; the alchemical names for Gold and Silver</note>. The *Rosarius* says: The shining bodies themselves, in which the tingeing streaks are found, tinge other bodies with true whiteness and redness once they are prepared.

### SECOND PART, CHAPTER 30
### D iij

For the incombustible white **sulphur** <term>Sulphur: In alchemy, this represents the active, masculine principle of combustion and soul, not just the chemical element.</term> belonging to **Silver** can, through greater cooking of the fire, become a red **sulphur** belonging to **Gold**. Therefore, it is said in the **Turba** <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between philosophers.</note>:

> When you see it completely black, then you shall know that a whiteness is hidden in the belly of that blackness; and then one must draw out that same whiteness from its blackness.

But in the second **decoction** <note>The process of heating or "cooking" the substance in a liquid</note> one must put the whiteness into its vessel with its instruments, and cook it with a gentle fire until it all becomes white. However, when you see this same whiteness in the vessel, then you should know that a redness lies hidden within the whiteness; and then one must not take it out, but rather cook it so long until it becomes entirely red.

But in this "red-making," two things must be diligently noted. First, that one should not pull the glass out, nor touch it. Secondly, that there should be a gentle and uniform warmth until the end, as was also indicated above. Therefore, **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says of both:

> When you have rightly prepared the impure **corpus** <note>body</note>, then put into it the fourth part of the **ferment**, set it in the sun and cook it; and the fire shall be gentle, and the vessel should remain undisturbed in its furnace until the entire time of the **fermentation** **Etheb** <note>A term likely derived from Arabic, here defined as the "fulfillment of the sun."</note>, that is, the fulfillment of the sun, is completed.

And **Alphidius** says:

> It is then rightly **congealed** <note>solidified or fixed</note> when you see the whiteness that surpasses all others; then you shall be certain that a redness lies hidden in the whiteness: and for that reason, you must not pull it out, but cook it well until it all becomes red:

However, it first becomes ash-colored and **citrine-colored** <note>A yellowish-orange stage</note> when the fire is increased. But all the **Philosophers** say that one must use a gentle fire. For even though the white **sulphur** is incombustible, it is still somewhat combustible, which the change of colors indicates before it is strengthened in the redness, as is seen from the above, and also like **Silver**.

Fourthly, you should know how to recognize when the **Lapis** <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is entirely perfect. Firstly, indeed, when its redness is no longer changed nor diminished, and that happens when it is entirely red, like blood **in actu** <note>original: "in actu," meaning in its completed, active state</note>, as **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemical author</note> says. Secondly, when it flows quickly in the fire like wax and is neither destroyed nor diminished. Therefore **Calid** <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, an early Umayyad prince associated with alchemy</note> says in the **Turba**:

> **Spiritus** <note>Spirit</note> is the water that draws out the **animam** <note>soul</note> from the **corpore** <note>body</note>, and that same **anima** is the **ferment** of the body: and it is just like a subtle, imperceptible smoke, and it is not present except by its **effect**: rather, its **actus** <note>actualization</note> is a revelation to the eyes, and it is a fire from the fire.

And for that reason, it must be drawn to the fire so that thereafter it does not fear the fire. And **Radianus** says:

> This is the very first test of the oil: that it does not smoke or crackle, but flows and **tinges** <note>transmutes or dyes</note> a plate of iron, copper, lead, and silver, and fixes itself with it, and does not fear the fire, nor is it diminished.

### NEW ROSARY

But Gold cannot become Silver unless it is first destroyed; when it is destroyed, it becomes black. But there is no path from the black to the citrine-red except through the white, just as there is no transition from the citrine-red to the white unless it first becomes black. The citrine-red, however, is nothing other than a change of the heaviness <note>The German 'schwere' refers to weight or density; here it suggests the material is becoming more 'concentrated' or 'weighted' with spiritual properties.</note>. For when the warmth acts upon the moisture, it first causes the heaviness; but when it acts upon the dryness and continues steadily, it causes the citrine-red. And therefore *Lilium* says: where the bodies <term>corpora: the solid metallic substances</term> are not divided, the colors of the souls do not appear. And further below it is said: The spirit <term>spiritus: the volatile, vaporous principle</term> and soul <term>anima: the life-force that connects spirit and body</term> are not united with the body in the proper way except in the white color. For then all the colors that can now be imagined in the world appear, and then they are confirmed into one color; that is, they come together in the whiteness.

The whitening, however, is the beginning and the foundation <note>original: "firmament"</note> of the whole Work; and it is no longer changed into many kinds of colors (namely those that are true colors) except only into the red, in which is the final end. In the cooking after the whiteness, one arrives at the citrine-red by increasing the fire in the governance <note>The 'regiment' refers to the controlled management of the furnace heat.</note>, and after the whiteness you can never err. Therefore *Mireris* says: One must first bury the earth in a piece of Egyptian cloth <note>original: "petia panni Aegyptii"</note>; afterward, one must make the compound <term>compositum: the mixture of alchemical ingredients</term> white, so that finally the tinting sulphur <note>original: "sulphur tingirendt"</note> becomes stable and constant, and afterward becomes red. For it becomes black twice, citrine-colored twice, and red twice. But the second red tints, which is not made except through the first whitening; if you wish to work philosophically—that is, if you whiten carefully—you shall be blessed. But if you see this happen quickly, a great terror will come upon you. And therefore *Raymond de Terminis* says: After the putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the 'death' or decomposition of the matter at the start of the work</term> you must make the sulphur, the determined critical days <note>original: "cretici"</note> of which are 90 at most; after that, no one can err any longer.

Therefore, thirdly, you should know that after the fulfillment of the whiteness, you should proceed to the perfect redness. For the redness of the Medicine <note>In alchemy, the 'Medicine' is another name for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> must be perfect, as *Geber* says, which happens in this way: after the incombustible sulphur of the two aforementioned bodies has been made white, that same sulphur is made red through greater cooking of the fire. For thus, Gold is made from Silver. And thus the white and red sulphur, as *Rosarius* says, are from one material of the metals, yet cooked in various ways. And *Plato* says: In every silver is red sulphur, and such sulphur is in the Sun <note>original: "Sole," representing Gold</note> and the Moon <note>original: "Luna," representing Silver</note>. *Rosarius* says: The shining bodies themselves, in which the tinting streaks are found, tint other bodies with true whiteness and redness, after they have been prepared.

## CHAPTER XXXI.
# That the precious virtue of our Stone is wonderful and innumerable.

After the Stone has been made red, it then tints all bodies <note>original: "corpora"; here meaning base metals</note> to perfection, as Alphidius says. For as Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist from Ferrara</note> says in chapter 5: It does not only change, but transforms in an instant, and is mixed without force—that is, by stripping away all superfluity and combustibility. And it is like the form of Gold <note>original: "forma Auri"</note> which possesses all the characteristics in potential and in act <note>original: "potestate & actu"; a scholastic way of saying it has both the hidden power and the visible reality</note> that mineral Gold has. And therefore it quickly makes all metals stable, lemon-yellow in color, entirely shining, heavy, and mute in tone or ring <note>Unlike base metals, pure gold makes a "thud" rather than a ringing sound when struck.</note>, and it has exactly the same virtue in <term>medicine</term> as true, pure, and precious gold.

And this form, among all forms in the world, is not only a quality, but also a quantity, for it is physical. And for that reason it is called a <term>Thiriac: theriac, an ancient "universal" medicine or antidote</term> and a poison of the philosophers; because it quickly coagulates and makes its Mercury stable, as if by "killing" it, and makes it perfect in the <term>tincture</term> and <term>Elixir</term> of other metals. And this is understood as the <term>sulfur of Gold: the active, coloring principle of the perfect metal</term>, which is not added from the outside, but is produced through great understanding and almost miraculously through the proper governance of the art from the <term>Quick-silver: mercury</term>, with which it is simultaneously purified through <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance into vapor and then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</term>. For according to Geber <note>A Latinized name for Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of chemistry.</note>, it is a tinting sulfur known only to Nature, and yet it is called an "addition of the tinting agent." Regarding this poison, Mundus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba"</note>: when this poison penetrates the body, it colors it with an unchangeable color, and the body never again leaves the soul <note>original: "anima"</note>, for it cannot be separated.

But you should understand that this Stone has the most magnificent virtues above all other stones, as Alphidius says. For its virtue is threefold in particular: The first is that it transforms Mercury, into which the fire has been placed, and all other metals quickly into true Gold, better than the...

## That the Medicine Can Be Multiplied Infinitely and Concerning Its Perfection

When the Medicine is perfect, it can be multiplied and increased almost infinitely <note>original: "in infinitum"</note> and without number. There are, however, three ways to multiply the same. The first is that one should dissolve <note>original: "solvier"</note> it many times through itself and coagulate <note>original: "coagulier"</note> it again. This dissolution and coagulation, however, occurs only with the Fire: for after the Medicine has been taught to withstand the Fire, the longer it remains in the Fire, the more its quality is increased and grows. Therefore, this dissolution is its melting like an oil, but it is coagulated again of its own accord in the Air. This is sufficiently evident from what was said before: for it also reaches its perfection through melting and congealing <note>original: "congeliern"</note>. For that reason, one shall dissolve and coagulate it again in this exact manner and for this reason, so that it becomes more perfect.

And this is what the *Rosary* <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a foundational alchemical text</note> says: The more the Medicine is dissolved, sublimated, and coagulated, the better and more abundantly it works. However, the dissolution <note>original: "solutio"</note> here is understood not as "water of dew or of clouds" <note>original: "Aquam roris vel nubis"</note>, as the fools believe, but rather that you transform the dry into the moist, and the coarse into the subtle as much as you can. For the work of dissolution was invented for no other reason than to make things subtle. And this is the opinion of *Geber* <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of chemistry</note>, who teaches how to make the fixed Stone volatile <note>original: "flüchtig"</note> many times through the methods of sublimation, and often stable until it flows and transforms into true gold in an instant. For from frequent repetition and reiteration arises the quality and increase, so that some Medicine can truly and perfectly transmute the body hundredfold, and some infinitely.

The second way is that one throws the Medicine onto a perfect body <note>A "perfect body" refers to gold or silver</note>, one part upon a hundred parts of the molten perfect body. After the projection <note>The act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten metal</note> has occurred, cover the crucible and place it in a furnace for several days; first make a gentle fire, then a stronger one, and always strengthen the fire, yet gradually and properly through its degrees <note>original: "Gradus"</note>, so that it all becomes one Medicine. In the same way, you can also multiply the Medicine when you throw one part upon 100 parts of raw heated mercury <note>original: "Mercurij crudi calefacti"</note>; then it will become the subtlest and reddest powder. And this is the opinion of *Alphidius* <note>An Arabic alchemical author often cited in medieval western texts</note>. And this projection can be repeated many times.

And therefore, the more it is projected / or the greater the quantity it is cast upon / the more it is diminished in its virtue.

And thus, from one part of the Medicine of the first degree, a thousand parts of an imperfect body are brought to perfection: and from one part of the third degree, only ten parts. For just as the Medicine is brought through much change / from corporeality, coarseness, and imperfection to spirituality and the most subtle nature / so, on the contrary, it is brought through many projections from its spirituality to the nature of a coarse body: because of the coarse parts / into which it is inseparably incorporated.

For the Medicine quickly penetrates the bodies with its spirituality and subtlety / and changes, digests, and disposes their matter <note>original: "Materia"</note> through its heat: and perfectly separates the pure from the impure / the coarse from the subtle / and matches the subtle and pure to itself / and transforms it into its substance.

PART TWO, CHAPTER XXXI.

the Medicine is projected over a body according to the proper weight and proportion / and the whole is placed in the fire / and strengthened through its degrees <note>original: *Gradus*; the stages of heat or steps of the process</note> / and dissolved and coagulated <note>original: *solviert und coaguliert*</note> multiple times / until it flows like wax. For thus, gradually, through the digesting power and the moving heat of the Medicine / everything is sublimated / and transformed into an entirely spiritual nature. Therefore, if the Medicine had been so greatly weakened during the projection / that it had no entry <note>original: *ingreß*; the ability of the Stone to penetrate and fuse with the metal</note> / an entry will be given to it / when the first part of the Medicine is added to it and cooked / with dissolving and coagulating / until it flows. However, the smaller the power of the Medicine is / the more tempered the fire must be at the beginning / and administered through the stages of our time. But if nothing were left over from the first and most perfect Medicine / that could be added / then one must act differently: which one should take great care to avoid / so that such a thing does not happen / because it is enough to have made the Stone once / and it is not necessary to repeat the work. For the Medicine, when it is finished in the Philosophical manner / is entirely and utterly capable of being multiplied to infinity <note>original: *in infinitum multiplicabilis*</note>.

The third way is as the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius*; referring to the alchemical text *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> intends / that one part of the white or red Medicine be added to the Stone or to new Mercury / which has never yet been used in the Work / and it should be placed in digestion as before / and cooked with putrefaction, sublimation, and fixation <note>original: *putrificiern, sublimiern und figiern*</note> until it all becomes a tinged oil <term>tinged oil: a liquid form of the Stone capable of "tinging" or coloring base metals into gold or silver</term>: then you have a perfect Stone again / and this happens in a few days / and with less cost, effort, and danger. Always carefully keep something back as a ferment <term>ferment: a small amount of the completed Stone used to "leaven" or transform a larger mass of base material</term> / both of the white and the red. And this careful consideration will relieve you of the preceding effort and labor. For it appears as if Raymond <note>Raymond Lully, a legendary alchemical figure</note> also intended this in the third distinction where he speaks of fermentation / at the beginning of the book: and in the *Practice of His Physical Tree* <note>original: *Practica sui arboris physicalis*</note>, chapter 2 / and also elsewhere among the wise Philosophers.

With these four grades of sublimation / which I have recounted to you above / the entire Mastery is accomplished with the help of God / who be blessed and praised in eternity / Amen.
